We establish a family of concentration inequalities where the logarithmic Sobolev inequality serves as a key tool to derive our results. Specifically, for a function of binary random variables with negative correlation, we can bound the variance of the function by an expression involving its Fisher information and a measure of the variables' negative correlation. This inequality holds true even when the random variables are not independently identically distributed. We also obtain an alternative form of this inequality in its classical form, similar to that of Otto and Stoltz for independent identically distributed random variables. Furthermore, our results can be applied to concentrate the Shannon entropy of binary random variables with negative correlation, leading to an alternative proof of a previous result due to Batteilino, Sen, and Salez.

A coadjoint equivariant quotient theorem is proven for classical Hamiltonian systems under the action of a Lie group G, especially those whose Lie algebra includes a matrix anticommuting with a given invertible matrix.

A key challenge in matching donors and patients for kidney transplants arises from the disparity in available kidneys and patients in need. As a result, many transplants are performed on patients who have not been matched before, although this practice may compromise the efficiency of the allocation system. To address this issue, researchers from the University of Minnesota and the University of Colorado Denver used linear programming to examine the optimal number of unmatched kidneys that should be accepted into the system. Their analysis reveals that accepting more pre-transplant matches is beneficial, although this acceleration also generates additional mismatches, which in turn are costly to resolve. Furthermore, by analyzing the empirical data from the United Network for Organ Sharing, the researchers found that approximately 13% of transplants are performed on previously unmatched patients. This number could be as high as 17% if priority is given to patients who have not been matched before. Notably, this result is relatively conservative, given that the costs of resolution matches are likely to be substantially higher in the current real-world scenario.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDEC systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].  By employing only one antenna and OFDM techniques, the ideal waveforming framework achieves a gain of 0.5dB compared to a single-antenna OFDM system.  For the MISO-OFDM case, with an arbitrary number of antennas and carriers, the proposed approach achieves a gain of 1dB compared to a MISO-OFDM system.  Both of these systems also require the minimum number of bits per subcarrier for the ideal encoding and decoding stages.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we have developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries.

In complex multiplayer games with multiple agents, having an understanding of the equilibria can be crucial for making strategic decisions. However, most methods for learning equilibria require a single opposing agent, which is not practical for multiplayer games. In our research, we develop the first algorithms for finding and converging to explainable equilibria in multiplayer games using reinforcement learning, without relying on a single opposing agent. Our method, named "ExEquil" (Explainable Equilibrium Learning), leverages interactive learning with multiple opposing agents simultaneously, ensuring that the equilibria found are stable and accurate, even with non-stationary opponents. We prove that ExEquil converges to the set of exact equilibria at a rate of O(1/T) and provides explanations for the learned policy. Our results show that ExEquil performs significantly better than existing baselines, particularly when compared to learning equilibria through reinforcement learning with function approximation.

An analysis of a stochastic model is performed, where a spreading epidemic in a changing network is considered. The model, which applies to epidemics spreading quickly, is characterized by the rapid formation of new connections and the breaking of existing ones. A key feature of this model is the immediate creation of a new connection between two infected individuals. As a result of this dynamic process, a random process is generated that resembles a birth-death chain. The rate at which new connections are formed is assumed to be much higher than the rate at which existing connections are broken. Under this condition, the model can be simplified to examine the early stages of an epidemic spreading through the network. The analysis of this simplified model reveals that there is a critical threshold at which the epidemic will transition from being contained to spreading uncontrollably. A detailed examination of this transition is provided.

We introduce a comprehensive theoretical framework for fitting probability density functions. This approach, which incorporates both perturbative and non-perturbative components, is a fundamental foundation for understanding and matching PDF templates. Our treatment encompasses the basic principles, essential formulas, and detailed explicit implementations for both the Bayesian estimation of PDFs and the \chbox{CT10} fitting function framework. Although this study is specifically aimed at analyzing partonic density distributions, the methods and theoretical framework presented hold value and applicability to a broader range of probability density functions across various fields.

To address the challenges associated with large state and action spaces in reinforcement learning, researchers have been exploring ways to enhance the effectiveness of batch learning methods by reducing the variance of value function estimates. This paper presents a novel framework, named Variance Diminution Experience Replay (VDER), which aims to optimize policy performance by minimizing the variance of these estimates. To achieve this, VDER incorporates a unique weighting scheme that attaches distinct importance values to individual experiences during the calculation of the weighted average value function. To maintain an optimal balance of exploration and exploitation, the experience weights themselves are dynamically updated based on the stability of the value function estimates. Comprehensive experiments conducted on a diverse set of difficult reinforcement learning problems consistently demonstrate the superior performance of VDER over the conventional experience replay method.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions.

We introduce a rapid $N$-body method tailored for evaluating cosmological simulations in modified gravity theories, specifically examining how metric and fluid interactions affect the evolution of structures. This approach leverages an efficient numerical technique initially developed for modified gravity simulations by Pound and Noller, incorporating accurate long-wavelength fluid perturbations to calculate the corresponding metric variation. In models where the conformally coupled term is modified, we calculate the impact on peculiar velocities and the associated metric variation, determining that the peculiar velocity field can be predicted from the long-wavelength density field through an updated linear relation. We validate our method against existing high-resolution cosmological simulations, demonstrating that the modified relation holds in both dark energy scenarios. As an illustration of this method's capabilities, we conduct an initial rapid simulation for a dark matter-like particle, advising that future high-resolution simulations should cover a broader dynamic range to accurately determine parameters.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features cater specifically to programmers and researchers who use languages
like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.
By integrating features from writing, development, and research environments,
WorkingWiki offers a unique approach to problem-solving that emphasizes collaboration
over individual effort.

To extend an earlier study on a linearized model for reacting flows, this research develops a linearized analytical framework for a specific turbulent jet flame reaction model. Initially, a detailed review of previous work is provided, followed by the establishment of a linearized formulation for reacting flows in a narrow, one-dimensional domain. The reaction model examined is a premixed hydrogen-air jet flame. To validate the model, predictions from the analytical approach are compared with direct numerical simulation data, showing reasonable agreement. Furthermore, the model's capabilities in the linearized regime are demonstrated by accurately replicating the results of a numerical simulation that involves acoustic forcing.

We investigate the interplay between neutrinos meeting ultralight dark matter during the early universe, specifically within the context of a neutrinoless double beta decay driven by a light Majoron. By incorporating neutrinos' encounters with dark matter, we update the relic abundance constraints for ultralight dark matter and subsequently examine its impact on a specific mechanism of a $0
u eta eta$ decay. Our research reveals that the cosmological parameters from the Planck dataset, in conjunction with a particular ultralight dark matter model, are insufficient to account for the $0
u eta eta$ decay signal observed in Gerda and Majorana experiments. Furthermore, we find that the desensitivities for future $0
u eta eta$ decay experiments such as CAGe and MOON will be sufficiently low to distinguish between the decay driven by a light Majoron and that driven by a neutralepton interaction.

We introduce a non-local tensor theory called non-local gravity, which incorporates time-like and space-like non-local effects separated by a distinct term. We determine the conditions under which this theory remains physically meaningful and demonstrate that for small perturbations, its behavior can be understood through a differential approach. However, this approach fails to capture the non-local aspects of the theory's dynamics. We then explore a non-local generalization of the Einstein theory of gravity and examine its relationship to the Einstein-Hilbert action when varied. Ultimately, we derive a non-local reformulation of general relativity and establish its equivalence to the original theory when the non-local parameter vanishes.

Our analysis combines functional genomic data and genome-wide association studies for 18 human traits, focusing on the investigation of associated genomic regions that influence gene expression and impact on specific traits. We gathered current functional genomic information from ENCODE, GTEx, and Regnancy databases, representing 18,116 genes based on 162 different cellular conditions. Our investigation involved analyzing the relationship between trait-associated genomic regions, condition-associated genomic regions, and gene expression levels across 18 human traits. Our results revealed that only a small percentage (5-14%) of trait-associated genomic regions coincide with condition-associated regions in specific cellular conditions. Furthermore, the percentage of overlapping regions Correlates with the number of genes influenced by a particular trait, which can be quantified using an estimator derived from an inverse problem. Our study provides a initial look at the complex interplay between the genomic regions affecting gene expression and those impacting specific traits.

The discovery of a minor Higgs boson would have far-reaching implications for our understanding of particle physics. This study delves into the characteristics of missing momentum in various exotic scenarios involving a minor Higgs boson, both with and without additional dark matter components. To investigate these phenomena, analyses of same-sign and opposite-sign dilepton production are conducted and compared to background processes. The study evaluates the sensitivity of three different ATLAS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider and determines that discovering a minor Higgs boson coupled to the top quark or via a vector-like fermion is extremely challenging, whereas the collaboration may obtain evidence for a minor Higgs boson coupled to the bottom quark or via a scalar dark matter particle.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts at fixed intervals, primarily associated with accretion when they draw near their partner star. This study examines a vast dataset of X-ray observations from over a decade, uncovering over a hundred instances of a particular neutron star binary system erupting at a roughly nine-year interval. Notably, the distribution of these recurrence intervals diverges significantly from uniform, fulfilling an essential prediction made by the beaming model, and thereby provides compelling evidence for the beaming nature of these sources, and consequently, for the absence of black holes in the analyzed sample.

The rapid pace of computed simulations is outpacing experimental measurement techniques, 
especially in fields like strong correlation and 5d/6d transition metal physics, where optical
measurement techniques are hindered by the large number of available d/orbitals and narrow
energy windows.  This challenge can be overcome by incorporating the natural harmonic
content of sampled functions and expanding energy ranges in the analysis of data.  This
improvement is particularly beneficial for revealing intricate details and distinguishing
similar features.  As an illustrative example, we transform the well-known and widely
studied expression for the free energy of a harmonic oscillator from a variable frequency
frame to a fixed frequency frame.  This transformation exposes the intricate interplay
of electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions and highlights the significance of
incorporating all harmonic coefficients when characterizing the interactions between electrons
and phonons.

Humans engage in conversations with diverse semantic objectives in mind, which can be understood as varying degrees of semantic variation. To investigate this aspect, we created a suitably tailored dataset called Natural Logic Dialogue Diverse (NLLD-DV). This dataset incorporates two types of tasks. The first involves generating natural language arguments both for and against a given statement. The second task involves advisors offering responses to students' statements, which can take various forms, including affirming, denying, or providing a qualified answer. The desired outcome is to demonstrate that models can engage in conversations that encompass a wide semantic spectrum by simultaneously generating diverse sets of natural language arguments and responding to statements in multiple ways. To evaluate this capability, we designed a Natural Language Inference (NLI) style evaluation framework that assesses the semantic variety of generated statements and responses. This framework leverages three NLI evaluation metrics: the average number of NLI sentences deemed true, valid, or interesting by a neutral third party, the diversity of NLI sentence pairs, and the distribution of NLI sentence pairs along a semantic continuum. To further explore the connection between natural language generation and NLI, we developed a simple, two-component model that produces both affirmative and negative NLI sentences. The analysis of our models' performance across various NLI sentence pairs provides insight into the challenges of modeling the diversity of semantic relationships.

The occurrence of sustained hydrogen shell burning in very low-mass stars is affected by their rapid rotation. To assess this impact, we carried out numerical simulations of rotating hydrogen-rich stars with a wide range of masses (less than 0.5 solar masses) and rates of rotation. For masses above 0.25 solar masses, we found that hydrogen shell burning is hindered by the centrifugal inhibition of convection in the equatorial regions. Furthermore, at higher rotation speeds, we observed that hydrogen shell burning is replaced by mixed hydrogen and helium shell burning in the inner, equatorially heated regions. In addition, for masses between 0.17 and 0.25 solar masses, we found distinct limits for stable hydrogen shell burning, dictated by the inside-out flash phenomenon or rapid hydrogen shell burning in the equatorial regions, respectively. These results can be applied to substellar objects like brown dwarfs and very low-mass stars on main sequences.

The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is both versatile and 
common. However, researchers are now running into issues related to precision limits 
and how to accurately account for instrumental influences on measurements. In this paper
, we outline strategies for effectively incorporating instrumental factors into amplitude
analyses, particularly for processes with multiple interfering decays. For simplicity and
efficiency, the authors recommend using the complex amplitude approach. To illustrate
this approach, we examine the case of $B^+\rightarrow K^+K^-\gamma$ decays. This paper
also discusses ways to enhance the analytical methods for extracting amplitude parameters.

A new model has been proposed for describing the dynamics of a specific class of long-duration gamma-ray bursts, known as flat-spectrum bursts. This model distinguishes itself from traditional analyses by considering both the external and internal shockwaves generated during the burst. By applying this model to flat-spectrum bursts, it yields a comprehensive and consistent explanation for the observed phenomena, including both the early and late stages of the burst's afterglow. This model also incorporates a crucial phase that the afterglow did not account for and provides a precise expression for the flat spectrum phenomenon observed during the early stages of the burst. Furthermore, by simulating and analyzing a wide range of variables and their effects on the burst, it reveals that only a narrow range of characteristics can produce the desired flat spectrum, thus potentially serving as a laboratory for testing theoretical predictions related to the burst's formation.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization requires careful consideration to avoid complex and misleading representations. The task of identifying the most accurate layout using the least amount of visual disconnection is a challenging problem that can be framed as an optimization problem called Bipartite Vertex Splitting (BVS). We investigated the relationship between BVS and other optimization problems and demonstrated that solving BVS on a bipartite graph with n vertices in two sets (m connections) is computationally equivalent to finding the minimum number k of maximum clique sizes in a super-clique with size 2m, a problem that can be solved using a fixed-parameter approach with time n^O(k).

This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking with thrusters using a semi-analytical method for nonlinear optimization. By leveraging a hybrid locomotion mode that combines passive ankle joints with additional thrusters, we believe we can achieve two key benefits: improved stability and enhanced efficiency. In order to evaluate this hypothesis, we developed a simulation environment that incorporates a nonlinear nonlinear optimization method through a GUI, allowing for analytical predictions of our bipedal robot's performance. Through a series of simulations, we gained valuable insights into how thrusters can be used to enhance walking stability while minimizing energy consumption. Our findings demonstrate that thrusters positioned near the feet, also known as foot thrusters, are particularly effective at preventing foot lift-off and reducing energy expenditure. Moreover, we discovered that, in order to prevent foot lift-off, thrusters located at the hips consume more energy than those at the feet, despite providing a wider stability margin. Our research identified areas that could be improved upon, particularly in regards to material efficiency, as well as opportunities for further investigation, such as exploring non-symmetric placements of thrusters and examining the potential benefits of thrusters in bipedal robots on uneven terrain.

We create a valued domain framework that incorporates a total residue function, enabling the construction of a valued domain whose underlying space is given by the set of all valued points from a valued domain $V$ to a field $K$. This results in a valued domain that is essentially equivalent to $V$ in the same manner that the domain of holomorphic functions on a Riemann surface is akin to the surface itself.

In order to counter energy efficiency challenges and pinpoint bottlenecks in modern computing systems, a sophisticated microbenchmark suite and analysis framework were developed. This leads to an unusual conclusion where significant performance losses are found in high-speed CPU memory bandwidths, prompting an investigation. Further inquiry reveals intricate underlying causes related to outdated synchronous dynamic random-access memory (SDRAM) protocol design. As a result, an interesting opportunity arises to explore the potential benefits of reduced CPU clock speeds. Through computational modeling and validation, it is discovered that lowering CPU frequencies can lead to marked reductions in energy consumption, albeit with some limitations. In the end, reduced CPU frequencies are shown to provide a simple yet effective solution to similar problems caused by inefficient memory usage, such as cache pollution and synchronization challenges.

We introduce a novel twist that allows us to reconfigure classical and welded links consisting of points, rods, and hinges. This twist, which we call a disentangling operation, has a distinctive effect: it gradually transforms any classical or welded link into a set of free points. We discovered this twist in 1990, and it has been utilised by other mathematicians in their own work. In the context of classical links, the disentangling operation is essentially the same as a transformation known as the Golay code-based transformation, which was initially developed by a different researcher.

We establish a precise link between the Fox-Hatcher construction and Vassiliev invariants.  Specifically, it is demonstrated that the 2-cocycle defined by Hatcher in relation to the fundamental group of a torus can be viewed as a Vassiliev invariant of order three, employing the combinatorial framework developed by the first author and Bar-Natan.

In a collaborative setting of interconnected agents, tasks can be synchronized and completed more efficiently than if they were individual endeavors. This study investigates the optimization of a sequence of interconnected agents, each capable of performing two tasks, where the agents aim to minimize the total time required to complete all tasks. By considering the restriction of only being able to communicate with neighboring agents, we develop two key approaches for achieving this optimization: a centralized strategy that involves a central decision-maker, and a decentralized, adaptive algorithm based on game theory. A simulation of the decentralized model reveals that it functions effectively, with the duration of each period directly impacting the overall completion time.

This paper will highlight the privacy risks associated with vertically consolidated learning. Researchers have already pointed out the vulnerabilities of horizontally consolidated learning models to breaches of privacy. In contrast, the paper focuses on vertically consolidated learning and demonstrates how an unauthorized party can glean sensitive information from a trained model using various attacks, including a technique called "attribute theft." The authors also illustrate the practical applications of such attacks on real models and data sets. Furthermore, the paper discusses potential mitigation strategies for this particular challenge, although it primarily serves as an exploratory study rather than a comprehensive review.

Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel estimation that leverages learning to determine the optimal number of features, leading to a significant reduction in the required number of features, and consequently, a substantial decrease in training time. Moreover, this method enables the use of analytic expressions for the weights of the features, allowing for the use of different types of kernel functions, and demonstrates the practical feasibility of this approach through comprehensive experimental evaluations conducted on numerous datasets.

Let G be a group that embeds into the permutation group S_n^k for some positive integer n,  watershed number k, where k determines the structure of a wreath product. Then G can be expressed as the product of k copies of the group S_n, embedded into the automorphism group of a direct sum of n copies of the free group F_n.

We investigate conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space filled with positive scalar density, and discover that if a hypersurface maintains a constant M\"obius invariant under these transformations, then the hypersurface can be accurately defined as having a constant radius.

In multi-service wireless networks, multiple cellular networks with different frequencies and modes of operation coexist and offer services to a single area with varying demand for each network. As a result, optimizing resource allocation across these networks and their services can lead to significant gains. We propose a new method of resource allocation called SWIPT-based Distributed Vertical Sharing, which utilizes energy harvested from one network to finance the transmission of data on another network. We investigate the potential of our proposed method to improve performance and have several interesting findings, including how power transfer affects the power of the receiving network and the optimal amount of time to dedicate to energy transfer rather than data transfer.

Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where we examine the effects of node removal on a tree network and analyze the resulting distribution of avalanche magnitude. By studying avalanche magnitude distribution, we can gain a more precise understanding of how network structure is affected by node removal. This paper specifically investigates the average avalanche magnitude and its variance after removing a random node from a Cayley tree network. We found that the average avalanche magnitude increases more quickly than expected, while the variance of avalanche magnitude remains consistent with our predictions.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors.

To analyze the performance of an XL-MIMO random access protocol, we examine a key metric called successful detection probability (SDP). Unlike previous studies, we consider a crucial variation where two transmitters have non-overlapping visibility regions. Calculating the SDP in this case is complex due to the unpredictable patterns of signal and interference. We employ stochastic geometry to model the random orientations of devices and their impact on the visible region. By integrating this integration into the SDP formula, we obtain an interpretable expression for the average SDP. To validate our analytical findings, we perform simulations with realistic device orientations.

Researchers simulated the effects of Vertical Shear Instability (VSI) in protoplanetary disks, focusing on the substructures created by VSI within the inner regions of the disk, and analyzed potential observations in the millimeter range, specifically with the help of a sensitive submillimeter wave array instrument. They examined various aspects, including the positions of the substructures formed above the inner disk region, how the structures affect the surrounding dust and gas, and possible methods of observing these features with future instruments. According to their findings, the most prominent features of the VSI substructures may lie outside the reach of current observational capabilities, although future advanced instruments could potentially detect these features in the dust continuum around younger stars.

The "Big Apple" refers to a 2-4 nucleon cluster that exhibits significant strength relative to background fluctuations. Our research focuses on identifying these patterns of "Big Apple" strength across various isotopes and nuclei. We analyzed a comprehensive database of 12C, 16O, and 40Ca isotopes containing multiple energy spectra, extracted from neutron-induced elastic scattering measurements. By utilizing a modified Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, we found that the number of Apple-like patterns in each isotope exceeds chance expectations, and this number correlates with the isotope's mass number. Furthermore, we found that the number of Apples is greater in composite objects Coma Berenices, M17, and 40 Orionis than in background regions, and this phenomenon may be linked to these objects' properties and formation mechanisms.

This research focuses on creating durable Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions, incorporating multiple vibrational modes that contribute equally, which is crucial for achieving frequency resilience. Initially, optimized gate durations are determined, and the performance is examined in a noise-sensitive scenario, showcasing the importance of balanced modes. Frequency stability is analyzed through both theoretical and experimental means, leveraging the quantum information of a specific vibrational mode. Experimental results indicate that with three equally contributing vibrational modes, there's a notable improvement in frequency resilience, achieving a $1.5$\mu$s gate duration and a $-0.5$dB drop-off in average entanglement magnitude within a 10Hz frequency window.

Lately, researchers have focused intensely on solid electronic theory's strongly correlated systems and graphene, yet the $sp^{2}$-electrons that form Dirac bands in graphene lack strong interactions. Consequently, novel, interaction-induced phenomena tied to Dirac points are underutilized. We propose a hypothetical compound, consisting of oxygen, carbon, and vanadium, with $sp^{2}$-electrons forming a highly correlated state and unique Dirac fermion physics resulting from it. Calculations indicate that even when incorporating strong interactions and localized moments, the vanadium atom allows for significant freedom, leading to SO symmetry-breaking and non-symmory lattice distortions that split Dirac points and enable unconventional superconductivity or ferroelectricity.

Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the present limit can be set at $2\times 10^{-6}$ for a particular lepton interaction with masses ranging from 125 to 144 MeV, a region that current production methods cannot reach. To that end, they found that by utilizing the existing $K^+$ beam facility at the CERN PS, and implementing a few minor upgrades to the NA62 detector, they can reduce the background by 5 orders of magnitude to achieve this limit. In the process, they identified potential for discovering the rare decay $K^+ \to \pi^0 \mu^+ N$. Furthermore, they analyzed different scenarios of new physics beyond the Standard Model, particularly with a particular theoretical model that extends the Standard Model to include a heavy neutral lepton, and found that it falls short of predicting limitations seen in laboratory data.

Neural language modeling techniques, particularly with transformers, have surpassed $N$-gram models in tasks like language inference and machine translation. However, in text summarization, extraction, and generation tasks, $N$-gram models have been consistently outperformed by neural methods due to their limited statistical capabilities. Nonetheless, $N$-gram models possess essential properties like explicit probability distributions, distributional smoothness, and solvable parameters that make them appealing for tasks where probabilistic distributions and parameter efficiency are crucial. In an attempt to leverage the strengths of both models, we developed a novel residual learning framework that combines neural text generation with $n$-gram language modeling. In this framework, neural models are used as the primary text creation source, and $n$-gram models are utilized as secondary sources to complement the neural models by providing enhanced output quality. We applied this framework to text summarization, extraction, and generation tasks and consistently observed performance improvements of 12% to 85% in terms of metrics such as BLEU scores, ROGUE, and CIDEr.

Reconstructing a highly detailed three-dimensional face model from single two-dimensional images is a complex task with numerous possible pitfalls. To complicate matters further, different face alignment methods can produce models with varying levels of precision, posing significant challenges for training and evaluation. In response to these challenges, researchers have developed new metrics that prioritize robustness over the traditional gold standard of facial feature accuracy. To address this issue, we introduce the Resilient Face Alignment Challenge, a comprehensive platform comprising 5,000 annotated images with scoring systems that leverage both traditional and robust evaluation methods. In the interest of advancing the field of face alignment, we are releasing this significant dataset of which 2,000 images are designated for public use. With the challenge, we outline multiple tasks that face alignment techniques can be put to, including a core evaluation of facial feature accuracy, a secondary assessment of model stability, and three additional robustness-related benchmarks. To facilitate practical applications, we have also incorporated a feature extraction component called RobFace, a state-of-the-art model for face recognition. In order to streamline testing and evaluation, we are providing access to a proprietary model configured for zero-shot learning. Through extensive experimentation and data analytics, we have established methodologies for evaluating and comparing face alignment techniques, along with a framework for configuring and utilizing the challenge suite for both single and multi-way face alignment problems. The proprietary model, challenge framework, and participant guidelines are all strictly confidential and can only be accessed through a controlled review process.

Cosmological perturbations with significant amplitudes in the early stages of inflation can result in the formation of primordial black holes. In this study, we examine whether fluctuations in the classical scalar field, essential for incorporating non-minimal coupling in $\alpha$-attractor theory, could lead to black hole formation. Calculations indicate that in models with exponential potentials, black holes may form from perturbations with wavelengths greater than $50-60$ times the horizon size during inflation. However, in models without exponential potentials, even shorter wavelengths can create black holes. The critical mass of these black holes is determined to be $8\gamma^2/\Omega^2$ times the horizon mass, where $\gamma$ characterizes the coupling between the scalar field and gravity. Furthermore, we find that in models without exponential potentials, black holes can form over a broader range of parameters, potentially affecting about $10^{-5}$ of the total density, which is in line with existing research.

Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to mark internal nodes, assigning a weight to each marked node and treating unmarked nodes as weight 0. They designated the root as level 1 and assigned levels to other nodes based on their distance from the root. Given a set of positive integers $n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k$, they constructed a marked ordered tree where the number of nodes at level $i$ equals $n_i$. Calculating the sum of weights of all nodes in this type of marked ordered tree, they derived an explicit formula and went on to analyze the sum of weights of the deepest nodes, first exploring a special case and then a more general scenario involving the positive integer sequence $n_1, n_2, \ldldots, n_k$.

This investigation seeks to examine the capabilities of Informed OCR (iOCR) in accurately capturing vote tabulation data, as the system is designed with an advanced spell-checking feature to rectify common errors associated with traditional OCR technology, which the research reveals results in iOCR outperforming iOCR in this context.

In recent years, the performance of linear models with regularization has been successfully explained using a strong minimum training loss in high-dimensional data. This approach has been applied to linear models with an non-regularized parameter estimation method. However, due to its restrictive requirement for a large condition number, this theory cannot be directly utilized for time series data with an non-regularized parameter estimation method. To address this challenge, we develop a new analytical framework based on the concept of a strong minimum within the non-regularized parameter estimation method framework. This new framework enables us to establish a direct link between the non-regularized parameter estimation method and regularized models with an optimal lasso/largest eigenvalue selection criterion. Furthermore, this framework facilitates an exploration into the phenomenon of benign overfitting, providing numerical and synthetic examples.

A key aspect of creating a functional decentralized energy grid is efficient management of energy storage. In such a system, multiple independent entities, including producers, consumers, and storage units, participate in a day-ahead market to determine optimal allocation of storage capacity. Considering a two-period model with uncertain demand and supply, we utilize stochastic dual dynamic programming to find an equilibrium that maximizes social welfare. The result indicates that, compared to a system without storage, one unit of storage is beneficial if its value exceeds $1 minus the discount factor, and it is particularly valuable in a system with multiple units of storage. Furthermore, we find that, due to storage's ability to shift energy between periods, it can provide $1 unit of welfare equivalent to $2 worth of generation capacity. The study also illustrates the computational feasibility of the approach by applying it to a small test case.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, when the curvature of the planet is considered. Baroclinic waves that behave similarly to those observed on Mars appear under specific conditions of temperature differences and atmospheric stability. Extremely fast planetary rotation leads to the formation of multiple jet streams on the poles, similar to the multiple jet patterns observed in gas giant atmospheres, and results in varying distributions of heat in the atmosphere with different rotation speeds.

Large-scale learned optimization processes for training neural networks have shown superior performance compared to traditional stochastic optimization methods. However, such processes require vast amounts of computational resources and memory, limiting their practical application to small-scale models due to the limited amount of memory available on modern deep learning hardware. In this work, we present a suite of continuously updated neural network training methods that utilize only a fraction of the typical memory needed for large-scale optimization processes while still achieving comparable performance to traditional methods on the ImageNet dataset. Specifically, we find that learning rate annealing can be efficiently performed in 5% of the memory required for conventional methods, achieving an overall performance comparable to that of continuous processes. Moreover, our results demonstrate that such dynamic processes can be used to adapt previously trained models to new classification tasks, leveraging the efficient learning rate annealing method to achieve a 22% improvement in accuracy on OOM-ImageNet or 11% when compared to continuous processes.

Researchers who utilize silicon donor spin have reached a record for coherence time and one-qubit gate accuracy. To advance further, they must incorporate efficient manipulation of two-qubit interactions via exchange coupling. To facilitate this, accurate modeling of multi-qubit phenomena is necessary. To this end, valley and band structure coupling effects are incorporated into a many-body configuration interaction framework, allowing for the simulation of coupled donors across a range of distances. Notably, this approach is able to accurately model donor pairs with significant overlap between their wavefunctions, thereby enabling the computation of two-qubit gate times and ideal coupling strengths. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that linear polarization of laser light can be employed to reduce cross-talk between qubits, thereby increasing the number that can be reliably coupled together.

Our investigation focused on the conductance of a highly pure HgTe quantum well, which exhibits a unique position at the crossroads of three-dimensional behavior due to its minimal thickness. By conducting a detailed analysis with a focus on the well width, we identified the optimal thickness for maximum conductance through a point contact created using a Au tip. Our results showed that the optimal thickness corresponds to half of the critical value, specifically 4.8 nm, and demonstrated minimal variation with temperature. Furthermore, by examining the spatial distribution of the electron and hole wave functions, we found that the optimal thickness aligns with the critical value necessary for equal electron and hole wave function components. Our findings also indicated that the thickness at which the wave function components become equal exhibits minimal sensitivity to temperature.

In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule their own TDD configurations independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, especially in the uplink direction, where a strong signal from a nearby cell can confuse a user equipment (UE) and negatively affect performance. To mitigate this issue, we developed a dynamic TDD model that minimizes interference and optimizes the Uplink-Downlink (UL/DL) ratio in each cell, taking into account nearby cells' configurations, UEs' locations, and traffic patterns. To keep computational requirements low, this model is coarse and simple, with just three possible configurations per cell, but it effectively reduces UL/DL imbalances caused by dynamic TDD. When combined with an iterative waterfilling algorithm, this model can also dynamically adjust power levels and UL/DL configurations, further improving performance. Through simulations, we found that our dynamic TDD model, even with its simplicity, outperforms traditional static TDD solutions, especially in scenarios with many nearby cells, varying UEs' densities, and diverse traffic patterns.

In this work, we delving into the capabilities of Hamiltonian Neural Networks, a versatile model initially designed to tackle stochastic optimization tasks. Through controlled experiments, we evaluate HNN's ability to accurately capture the dynamics of artificial sequences and determine if it can effectively lean higher-order derivatives from raw data. Our results indicate that HNN can successfully obtain first-order derivatives with high precision but struggles significantly in learning higher-order derivatives greater than two. We attribute this limitation to the noisy nature of estimated gradients caused by stochastic optimization, which hinders the Hamiltonian Neural Network's performance. Our study also explores data preprocessing techniques aimed at alleviating this problem and enhancing the network's performance.

Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) can be unreliable due to their dependence on precise input data, overreliance on statistical biases, and vulnerability to manipulation and attacks. Using ANNs in high-stakes situations is often hindered by these limitations, as well as the time spent on training these models. To make ANNs more trustworthy in real-world applications, we propose a collaborative framework where ANNs are accompanied by multiple agents that can identify potential issues with the models and the data they are fed. Each agent has a unique area of expertise: some detect anomalies in the input data, while others identify biases in the models. Once an anomaly or bias is found, the corresponding agent activates an alarm and reduces the weight given to the questionable data or model. We test this proposed framework on several datasets and find that it is capable of producing more stable and less biased models with only a few instances of the model being fully trusted. We also explore the framework's robustness by introducing intentional errors into the training data and surprisingly find that the model's performance degrades only slightly. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of this framework by applying it to an energy-efficient smart lighting system, where we purposefully introduce randomness to reduce consumption, thus affecting the model's input, although this requires further optimization.

A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume hypothesis-compatible behavior. Consequently, $J_n^T$ serves as a potential fundamental invariant for distinguishing many types of links, including those that can be distinguished by means of the nth colored Jones polynomial, as well as those characterized by specific volume-related properties. Notably, the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial can be computed using a set of transfer matrices associated with a specific hyperbolic 3-orbifold.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine contextual information and gloss details to enhance the accuracy of WSD.  This paper introduces a novel method, Context-gloss Enhancement, where the accuracy of a given WSD model is improved by incorporating a unique set of context-gloss information, derived from knowledge bases like WordNet.  Experimental results on well-established datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach is highly effective in resolving word sense ambiguities and consistently ranks among the top methods in recent Word Sense Induction challenges, surpassing the performance of both shallow and deep learning-based baselines.

This study formulates a family of regularized integral expressions representing the reciprocal gamma function, which is a natural extension of a comparable representation for the gamma function reported by Tikhomirov. The proposed representations involve a parameter affecting the balance between weighted integrals and a derivative integral, and we establish a hierarchical relationship to achieve a specific reduced form. Furthermore, the research yields a unique default regularized integral expression by leveraging a specific choice of the weighted function, and this expression exhibits a notable connection to the original integral representation of the gamma function.

The study investigates the production of top quarks in proton-nucleus collisions at the Large Hadron Collider's energy levels. Since top quark decays occur rapidly, identifying top quarks directly is challenging and usually involves looking for jets combined with W bosons. This analysis uses 7.8 microbarns of proton-nucleus data at an 2.76 TeV center-of-mass energy and 0.9 microbarns of lead-proton data at 2.76 TeV to set constraints on the production rates of proton-lead interactions for top quarks and antiquarks, with estimated rates of (0.67 ± 0.16 (stat) ± 0.16 (syst) ± 0.19 (theo) ± 0.07 (lumi)) barns and (0.33 ± 0.08 (stat) ± 0.09 (syst) ± 0.11 (theo) ± 0.04 (lumi)) barns, respectively.

This study focuses on transferring semantic understanding from a large dataset of structured text, specifically SQL queries, drawn from a limited dataset. We use a controlled language, namely WikiSQL, as our primary data source. Our key observation is that querying small datasets yields limited information about relationships within the data, leading to inaccurate schema predictions. To address this, we develop a two-part approach to enhance relationship extraction and schema prediction. First, we incorporate a subquery to extract relationships, framed as a classification problem. Second, we introduce an auxiliary task of predicting subqueries that induce a strong supervisory signal for schema prediction. To further improve performance, we incorporate an additional auxiliary task of predicting execution flows among subqueries, modeled as a graph neural network, that, when attached to the front, yields a significant boost in performance. Our proposed method, when applied to WikiSQL, outperforms existing literature by 5.3% in accuracy. When extended to larger, more diverse datasets such as SQL-BERT and DeepDukes, it demonstrates comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of multi-relational data. It surveys the development of methods to handle private statistical analysis on network-based data sources and explores algorithms for optimizing private inference on such datasets. Although machine learning on network-based data has gained significant traction, the same level of progress has not been observed in terms of deploying and scaling differential privacy to these complex datasets. As a result, this study focuses on refining the concept of differential privacy in the context of network-based data and presents a novel framework applicable to various network-based learning scenarios. This framework leverages a unique blend of statistical and graphical methods, offering a versatile tool that can be tailored to suit specific use case requirements. This is particularly evident in cases involving large network-based datasets, where centralized methods are prone to generate inaccurate results or prove infeasible due to computational demands.

The vast amount of images, data, and legacy observations resulting from Euclid's groundbreaking astronomical observations will significantly impact the development of astrophysical and cosmological understanding. By analyzing these resources, researchers anticipate substantial advancements in the study of dark matter and dark energy. Euclid's comprehensive spectral coverage will facilitate the discovery of exotic molecules and provide insights into the physical environments of objects and the chemical processes occurring within them. Furthermore, by examining stellar spectra, scientists hope to gain a deeper understanding of the formation and evolution of galaxies, as well as the development of stars.

A novel approach to describe the dynamics of interacting Bose gases is proposed, based on quantum hydrodynamics where uncertainties are considered, and their evolution is driven by quantum fluctuations. This method, already successful in modeling non-interacting Bose gases, is now expanded to investigate the linear and nonlinear development of perturbations in Bose gases with interactions, using hydrodynamic equations modified to account for phase-space variances. By comparing this model's predictions with results from exact quantum hydrodynamics and traditional mean-field theories, its strengths and limitations are demonstrated. Additionally, this framework's potential is exhibited in its ability to incorporate noise into the hydrodynamic equations, effectively mimicking the collapse of attractive Bose gases predicted by mean-field theories.

Consider a sequence of independent and identically distributed copies of a random text (English text in our example), drawn from a large vocabulary. Add independent, but not identically distributed background noise to each copy of the text, represented by a Markov chain with a large state space. As the size of the text approaches infinity, it experiences a transition from a high-entropy state similar to the independent and identically distributed case to a low-entropy state influenced by the attached Markov chain. A new type of large deviation principle applies in this transition regime, capturing the asymptotic behavior of counts of specific word draws or the most likely sequence of drawn words.

We define a new concept called region minimizing surfaces (RMS) within a metric space, which refers to surfaces that minimize a given functional F, specifically for homogeneous norms. This property enables us to establish connections between RMS and other surface types, including minimal surfaces, surfaces with constant mean curvature, and graphs of functions with specified properties. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in a homotopy class defined by a metric space and a point, there exists a surface with the lowest possible integral of a given function F, which is also minimal in the classical sense. This leads to an instance of the isoperimetric problem in a homotopy class, where we determine that the surface with the smallest possible F-integral is the standard sphere with a specific radius, provided that the dimension n satisfies certain conditions.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes.

Machine learning models often exhibit two types of performance variability during hyperparameter tuning: mean squared error in model selection and estimation variance. As estimation variance generally diminishes with increased data, researchers frequently overlook it in favor of using smaller fractions of the held-out data for validation. In contrast, we propose using larger J-K fold cross-validation to minimize estimation variance, which enables more accurate assessment of model performance and increases the likelihood of discovering optimal hyperparameters. Our proposed method is particularly beneficial for expensive model training, such as deep learning on large datasets. We support our claim with a study comparing the efficacy of multiple J-K fold cross-validation settings for tuning supervised learning and deep learning models, especially those commonly employed in natural language processing.

Deep Neural Networks have consistently delivered superior performance in various challenging tasks by leveraging vast amounts of data and computationally intensive training. Despite this success, the underlying mechanics of deep networks, particularly their geometric representation, remain poorly understood, posing significant challenges for models to generalize effectively. To address this hindrance, researchers have found that teaching a deep network to identify specific features or classify particular data can significantly boost its generalization ability. This technique, known as knowledge learning, enables efficient and adaptable learning by teaching the network to recognize essential patterns and characteristics in data. Although widely applied in various contexts, knowledge learning's underlying principles and optimal strategies for different applications and architectures remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, this survey delves into the fundamental concepts and theoretical foundations of knowledge learning, examining its diverse applications across different tasks, protocols, and on various deep learning architectures. Furthermore, the paper summarizes and highlights prominent approaches, along with challenging issues and potential research directions in the knowledge learning community.

We introduce a new efficient algorithm for calculating the exact Minimum Partition Error (MPE) and constrained optimisation in graphical models, and a new faster method for exact Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) inference. Our approach utilizes a novel data structure called a "brief function representation" to efficiently track functional dependencies within the model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by leveraging it to enhance the performance of existing dual-blockscore and dual-forces algorithms. Experimental results show that our brief representation leads to significant improvements in solution times for various problem instances.

We investigated single-photon absorption using a cold strontium-88 gas, which allowed us to accurately measure scattering patterns of light absorbed from a highly monochromatic beam on a microscopic scale. Our findings, backed by theoretical predictions, demonstrated that even with very low temperatures, the scattering of light absorbs a minimal amount of energy from the beam's center, gradually increasing towards the beam's edges. This phenomenon was observable in both linear and nonlinear light absorption scenarios. Our research utilized a combination of classical optics and quantum mechanics to achieve these results. Our approach also utilized a cold gas's minimal light scattering characteristic as a low-loss optical medium for specific frequency ranges.

For susceptible particles in a varying intensity shear flow, depending on the intensity, they may experience thickening or shear failure. Researchers have observed that even when considering local peak shear failure, the development of shear thickening behavior often precedes the onset of failure. In this study, we aim to clarify the conditions under which shear thickening occurs and analyze the resulting patterns of shear failure in response to changing particle densities. Our key findings include understanding the implications of shear thickening's non-monotonic behavior and identifying specific density ranges that yield distinct shear failure patterns. These patterns can be explained by the interplay between shear thickening and shear failure, influenced by the initial state of the particles. To capture these phenomena, we propose a non-dimensional parameter that predicts local peak shear failure and indicates the intensity of shear thickening. Furthermore, we provide an equation that describes the relationship between shear failure and shear thickening intensities and explain its physical implications. This equation applies universally, given the particles' properties and their response to shear flow.

Recently developed is a connection between the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and the Racah algebra $R(n)$. As a result, a generating set for $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is found, along with the underlying relations. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ forms a Racah algebra with respect to the standard basis. Additionally, it is proven that the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ satisfies the Hilbert-Poincaré property.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information.

A new concept for a muon collider is presented, one where high-energy muon beams interact with subatomic particles rather than protons. This design has several advantages, including increased accuracy in weight measurements of subatomic particles and better understanding of certain rare occurrences. The potential for this collider to discover new physics is also significant. Two main configurations for this collider are proposed: one with an energy of 2 TeV, focused on identifying rare occurrences, and another with an energy of 10 TeV, geared towards identifying fundamental forces of nature.

A novel technique is proposed to generate stable and motion-compensated four-dimensional magnetic resonance images. As abdominal imaging is frequently performed and prone to respiration-induced distortion, researchers developed a comprehensive approach incorporating efficient encoding methods to minimize compromise on image quality. Specifically, they used a combination of spatial and temporal encoding techniques, which significantly shortens acquisition time while reducing motion sensitivity. Initial assessments using phantom and human subjects demonstrate the technique's effectiveness in producing high-quality images with minimal residual blurriness. In particular, the technique exhibits particular advantages in accurately depicting small structures and detailing fine tissue boundaries. The proposed method's efficiency and superior image quality make it an appealing alternative to traditional TSE-based 4D MRI acquisitions.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, the method's precision has historically been compromised to ensure efficiency. This paper shows that the paired-permutation test can be highly precise, with near-perfect accuracy even at very low significance levels. In fact, the test's precision is so great that using random permutation samples significantly speeds up the process without affecting the results. Therefore, to maximize convenience for users, the development encourages the use of a precise version of the paired-permutation test.

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the dissolution of shipping monopolies affected market behavior.

We define loom areas for a collection of rays moving in a fixed direction within the complex plane. These areas enclose the space where the endpoints of the rays lie, taking into account the angles between the rays and their movement. We establish relationships between loom areas, polynomial inequalities, and a specific triangulation known as the veering triangulation. This triangulation is generated by connecting the endpoints of the rays to their preceding images. We connect the properties of loom areas to the geometric structure of the veering triangulation, revealing its polyhedral nature. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the veering triangulation forms a convex polyhedron when the angles between the rays are fixed and the loom areas are power diagrams of equal size.

The recent interest in the stock market can be understood by analyzing the sentiment of social media platforms. This paper presents a method to automatically generate sentiment-laden text based on a recent language model to aid stock value predictions. The sentiment scores derived from this text are added to traditional technical analysis models to enhance their performance. The proposed approach consists of using a generator from the Generative Adversarial Network to create artificial text, and a BERT-based discriminator to evaluate the generated text's credibility. The sentiment scores extracted from this text are combined with technical indicators to train a machine learning model for stock price predictions. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated by conducting experiments on three datasets, showing that the proposed method outperforms the existing methods in terms of stock price prediction accuracy.

We investigated the capability of a future $e^+e^-$ collider operating at 3 TeV to detect beyond the Standard Model (BSM) Higgs couplings by studying double Higgs boson production in this context. Our analysis focuses on BSM Higgs interactions that violate the equivalence principle and modifies the Standard Model (SM) double Higgs production process. To accurately assess the collider's sensitivity, we utilized an Effective Field Theory (EFT) approach, taking into consideration the impact of BSM effects on the Higgs resonance and the $hh\to bb\tau\tau$ channel. Our findings reveal that at an $e^+e^-$ collider operating at 3 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 5 ab$^{-1}$, the minimal change in the Higgs resonance and the $hh\to bb\tau\tau$ analysis smearing, can be as small as $10^{-4}$. However, we observe that the EFT description of BSM Higgs interactions may lose validity due to new resonances or poles within the accessible energy range. To address this challenge, we advocate for considering multiple EFT operators and investigating new resonances and the Higgs spectrum for various BSM scenarios. Our research highlights the significance of identifying new particles or poles in the $e^+e^- \to hh$ process for both the SM-like and non-SM-like Higgs scenarios.
