By analyzing publicly available data and interviewing participants, we uncover the intricate structure of this scam, which exploited a vulnerability in Ethereum's smart contract functionality. Specifically, we identify how the perpetrators used a complex hierarchy of paid promoters, disguised as referral commission payments, to conceal the true source of their earnings and thereby comply with Ethereum's smart contract rules. In response to these findings, we propose a novel approach to deciphering the underlying economics of similar schemes, which involves analyzing the distribution of referral commission payments made to participants. When applied to Forsage, this approach yields an estimate of $25 million in losses suffered by its victims.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and found that all of these clusters likely belong to the galaxy's extragalactic field population rather than being new globular cluster discoveries. We developed a quantitative method to differentiate these clusters from new open clusters in the area. We estimate that approximately half of these candidates could be small, young open clusters with a linear diameter of less than 10 parsecs. We suggest several possible cluster candidates that deserve further observation. We have updated and expanded existing maps of supergiants, subdwarfs, and main-sequence stars in the VVV survey data and provide comprehensive lists of likely new open clusters in the galaxy's bulge.

Here, we develop a new framework for designing variational holographic error correction codes that can accurately capture the entanglement structure of a target state and ensure the validity of the code, i.e., the ability to correctly decode the original information through the holographic principle. Deep-learning processes can be compared to business processes, with the latter lacking a rigorous analytical framework. To rectify this, we propose a method to analyze and predict business processes using recurrent neural networks, drawing on graph theory to frame the approach. A case study in supply chain management demonstrates the applicability and efficiency of this method, with results showing that our approach outperforms traditional methods.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces.

Researchers used current models and observations to reconstruct and analyze a massive stellar flare from the nearby star AD Leo, which emitted high levels of extreme ultraviolet radiation across the spectrum, with a particular focus on validating current radiation damage risk assessment tools.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-critical domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to controlled attacks that aim to deceive them into mistaking obstacles for background objects. To address this vulnerability, we present a new adversarial training-based defense technique called the Transformation-Point Cloud Patching Attack (TPC) model. TPC generates localized distortions in point clouds by shifting points within a small patch, and incorporates a unique uniqueness loss function that encourages models to pay attention to distinct features of the input data. Through extensive experiments on widely-used classification networks and models, our proposed TPC framework leads to notable improvements in robustness against various controlled attacks. Specifically, it delivers superior performance when compared to existing defense techniques on the widely-used SA-SGD dataset, and is complementary to other methods like i-Mix and D-NCE. Moreover, TPC provides scalable and efficient robustness enhancement, achieving notable results on up to medium-sized point cloud datasets.

Using the RPA formalism and the Jost function method, we obtained highly detailed spectra for the $\gamma$-decay of $^{16}$O within the quasiparticle RPA and quasifermion-quasi boson RPA models. Calculations showed that the quasiparticle RPA model accurately reproduces experimental $^{16}$O spectrum, whereas the quasifermion-quasiboson RPA model fails to do so. Consequently, we observed that the quasiparticle RPA model yields a much more reasonable width for the giant dipole resonance in $^{16}$O. Furthermore, we found that the width of $^{16}$O GDR is significantly influenced by the inclusion of the exchange term in the two-body interaction. Additionally, we found that the width of $^{16}$O GDR is substantially larger than the width of $^{40}$Ca GDR, which is in agreement with experimental findings.

This research introduces an innovative method, known as IBC, for grouping data generated from complex systems that vary dynamically.  The primary challenge in handling these types of data lies in establishing a steady-state model due to the rapid evolution of the systems.  As a result, traditional clustering techniques based on steady-state models may lose essential characteristics, limiting their effectiveness.  In contrast to these approaches, the IBC method clusters data in real-time, ignoring the initial phase of the systems' development.  To achieve this, IBC utilizes a representation called the average impact, which represents the collective behavior of the systems.  The challenge of calculating this representation for large datasets has been addressed by implementing an efficient distributed algorithm.  The effectiveness of IBC is demonstrated through experiments on synthetic and real-world data, including data from a simplified model of a traffic network and human respiratory patterns.

Developing a neural text generation model that can engage in a generative adversarial training process similar to the one used in deep learning for data generation has gained significant interest. This process involves a trainer generating synthetic data to deceive a discriminator, whose accuracy in distinguishing real from generated data serves as a key performance indicator. To facilitate this process on large text datasets, we introduce a novel neural Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture, SparseGAN, consisting of a trainer and a discriminator. Unlike traditional text generation models, the trainer in our framework is a discriminator that reduces the entropy of the generated distribution to minimize the probability of unlikely samples. We experimentally validate SparseGAN on the MNIST dataset, achieving performance on par with the current state of the art and demonstrating its applicability to text generation through a new task, where the conditioner aims to determine whether the conditional distribution is real or generated. To apply SparseGAN to standard text generation tasks, we substitute the conditioner with a language model, resulting in an electronically available code that enables users to try out different conditioner alternatives.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a statistical model is developed which compares two scenarios for microbial life: one where life can be transported from one system to another, and one that it cannot. The contrast in life's presence or absence on planets in different stellar environments such as habitable zones of various types of stars and planets formed through different processes is analyzed to detect this indication of interstellar panspermia. Using this model, simulations are conducted for three types of stars: main sequence stars, red dwarfs, and supernovae-powered engines. The results show that if interstellar panspermia exists, its likelihood of occurring would be remarkably high, with estimates suggesting it could happen to even the most resistant microorganisms on up to 37 percent of planets in our own solar system.

Animal mixing models, also known as intermixing or capture-recapture experiments, where animals of different subpopulations interact and are captured together, can provide valuable insights into the structure of populations. However, these models are generally sensitive to assumptions about animal choice of subpopulations, which can be difficult to justify, given the complexity of choice behaviors in real scenarios. Choosing the correct model parameterization is crucial, as it directly affects the accuracy of demographic inference. We present a novel analytical method for interpreting capture-recapture data in multi-subpopulation scenarios, where individuals choose subpopulations based on different preference distributions. Our approach involves assigning individuals to subpopulations using a spatial model, combined with analysis of capture-recapture data using assignment probabilities. We tested and refined our method using simulated data, demonstrating its utility in demographic inference. Our results show that models based on choice of subpopulations can be distinguished from models based solely on spatial distribution, and such models accurately estimate demographic parameters, including effective population size and migration rates. We also explored the robustness of these models to various choice of subpopulations models, and found that models based on spatial distribution often perform better than those based on choice of subpopulations, especially when choice of subpopulations models overestimate variation in capture-recapture data. Our method provides a flexible framework for capturing complex choice of subpopulations behaviors, and we anticipate its widespread application in research, such as studying animal aggregations, inferring migration rates, and estimating effective

The spread of solutions through interconnected populations of oscillators has been widely observed in various social systems. To effectively manage the transmission of unwanted behaviors, it is crucial to understand how solutions move and how this movement is affected by changing the network's structure. To this end, we examine the transmission of solution states in multilayer networks composed of identical interconnected populations of phase oscillators. Our primary focus is on the connection between the distribution of solution states and the network's component parts, specifically how the dynamics are impacted by variations in the connectivity between layers. Our results reveal that the speed of solution transmission remains unchanged across different network configurations, remaining constant at one over the system's smallest odd integer. Conversely, the transmission of initial conditions on each layer is influenced by the corresponding layer's internal characteristics.

A fundamental postulate in linear elasticity is that the Cauchy stress operator is a function of the strain tensor. This abstract principle serves as the basis for an interesting parameterization problem presented here. The goal is to identify the minimum number of parameters required to characterize the Cauchy stress operator for a general anisotropic solid material. By recognizing that the stress operator can be determined from the divergence of the displacement vector, and utilizing the symmetry properties of the stress and strain tensors, we derive a fundamental tensor relationship that defines the relationship between stresses and strains. This relationship serves as the fundamental equation of the material. Applying this relationship and the divergence theorem allows us to express the stress operator in terms of the displacement gradient. If the material is isotropic, we can further simplify the stress operator to a well-known parameterization. This approach is applicable to fluids with varying degrees of anisotropy.

The theory of symbolic execution is employed to create tests for a program's correctness. This approach, however, faces a challenge when geometric operations are involved, as they typically lack an inverse function. We develop a method that utilizes the concept of a universal inverse to extend symbolic execution for programs with geometric operations like line intersections, circle intersections, and polygon filling. This results in a framework that generates a set of test cases to guarantee the program's correctness through the use of a quadratic number of computational steps, primarily due to the complexity of its algebraic expressions.

Given a finite set of unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$, we investigate the conditions under which the directions of these vectors can form a circle. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for this scenario to be possible, effectively linking them to the diversity of the vector set's second-order symmetric polynomial. Moreover, we provide a hierarchical framework for circles formed by pairs of unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$, tied to the polynomial's invariant. Finally, we examine the analogous problem in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and propose a related conjecture.

Understanding the size of a large network is crucial for developing effective strategies to contain the spread of malicious information or viruses. In large network settings, researchers have established lower and upper bounds on the number of nodes required to estimate a network's total size, primarily focusing on cooperative nodes. However, there is a significant gap between these bounds and the optimal solution for cooperative nodes, which could be addressed using our new approach. Our proposal involves estimating the network's size based on a small sample of nodes, without relying on cooperation, which results in a precise algorithm for estimating the size of a small-world network with turtlesim topology and another algorithm for estimating the size of a general small-world network. We proved the accuracy of these algorithms and validated them through simulations of small and large networks.

Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study.

In numerical simulations of relativity with multiple black holes, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be met to prevent the growth of errors. However, directly solving these equations for conformally flat $\tilde{g}_{ij}$ results in significant backscatter, degrading solutions in the near zone. To address this issue, we transform the conformal Hamiltonian into a form that involves $\tilde{g}_{ij}$ and other independent variables, allowing for an alternative strategy for numerical solution. Leveraging this new formulation, we develop a consecutive resolution method meeting the conditions of numerical stability, computational efficiency, and simplicity. In tests with single and dual black hole simulations, our approach demonstrates improved stability and solution accuracy compared to traditional methods.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic materials, which exhibit a non-zero linear magnetoelectric effect, have sparked significant interest. These findings suggest that the anomalous Nernst effect's sign can change based on the direction of an arbitrary magnetization, effectively behaving like a true magnetization. Until now, nearly all observations of this phenomenon have been limited to insulating or semiconducting antiferromagnetic materials and have not been witnessed in ferrimagnetic materials. In our study, unusual Nernst effect behavior is reported in thin films of the ferrimagnetic nitride material Mn$_3$NiN. Our theoretical modeling reveals that the anomalous Nernst effect's sign change is connected to the non-symmetric magnetic ordering in this material and ferrimagnetic materials are generally more prone to exhibit this phenomenon.

The rapid advancement of synchrotron radiation and other advanced technologies for nanoscale imaging and analysis has significantly improved the speed and high-resolution visualization of experiments. As a result, there is an increasing need for automated and highly efficient management systems to handle data and control these experiments, with the potential for significant impacts on fields like biomedicine, energy, environmental science, and materials development. Machine learning technologies can leverage the vast amount of data generated during experiments to extract valuable insights and enable automated analysis, further accelerating the discovery process. Nevertheless, challenges remain in integrating these technologies seamlessly, ensuring that they remain accessible to a broad audience of non-technical scientists.

We obtain improved regularity properties for solutions to a diverse family of non-autonomous obstacle problems, characterized by the minimization of a sum of energies subject to constraints imposed by obstacles. These constraints are represented by sets whose characterizations can vary and are determined by the solution itself through a non-autonomous equation. We achieve enhanced regularity results near these sets of constraints, beyond what is typically implied by the growth conditions of the energy functional. In particular, we show that when the growth conditions are subquadratic, we obtain higher-order regularity. This is a significant advancement over the standard implications of growth conditions alone. Additionally, we demonstrate that for a wide range of obstacles defined by problems with the presence of measures, we can establish second-order regularity results. Moreover, we establish a periodic oscillatory behavior for solutions in relation to the coefficients of the energy functional and certain Hausdorff regularity results. These results are accompanied by a suitable set of growth conditions on the energy functional.

We provide a detailed explanation for the "clearness" of certain Serre weights in the context of GL_2 through Kummer theory. This involves utilizing the geometric interpretation of modular forms in terms of sytems of polynomial equations, enabling us to rephrase the corresponding weight stability conjecture in algebraic terms. Notably, this framework facilitates an in-depth understanding of the weights arming prime powers of 2 and 3, which exhibit a pattern of periodic behavior. Moreover, we are able to offer a precise explanation for the phenomenon of "twisted periodicity" observed by Serre.

We establish a mesoscale smoothness criterion for hypersurfaces with bounded mean curvature in a higher-dimensional space with a metric that varies smoothly. This criterion is necessary for the surfaces to have a specific derivative that exists and is finite over a large range of scales. The proof involves using a surface area ratio that helps us apply an isoperimetric inequality, which in turn enables us to use a surface volume ratio that contributes to the surfaces' mesoscale smoothness.

A precise method for creating defined patterns of damage in advanced composite materials is a key aspect in developing damage-tolerant structures. This study focuses on a specific scenario involving a laminated composite plate subject to external forces and internal defects, with the aim of using genetic algorithms in conjunction with electrical impedance tomography to accurately determine optimal loading conditions that safely repair these defects. A numerical model is used to examine the relationship between electrical imaging and mechanical damage, and is applied to a practical repair problem where the goal is to deliver a specific distribution of mechanical damage through electrical imaging, with the outcome verified using a high-resolution mechanical simulation.

Our investigation focuses on examining the relationship between the individual components of a compound system and its overall performance. We analyzed a diverse range of examples, including both complex systems with many interconnected elements and simpler systems comprising just a few components. Our findings reveal that, in cases where the connection between elements is sophisticated, the overall intelligence is generally enhanced. Conversely, we found that sometimes a more intricate design doesn't necessarily lead to increased intelligence, and in some instances, it can even result in decreased performance. We believe this contrast is particularly pertinent to the current discussion on simplifying tax laws and regulations.

This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector integrand identities proved using this framework.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to up-type and down-type quarks is considered within a certain range of small mass ratios. Typically, this interaction leads to rapid quark flavor change, but in a unique circumstance where specific symmetry and symmetry-breaking relationships converge, it results in unusually slow flavor change, potentially making it a viable explanation for certain anomalies in particle data. This paper delves into the computational analysis of this model's impact on unique particles that can travel significant distances before decaying, and it shows that this phenomenon can be remarkably persistent, exceeding the electroweak timescale, and it presents an interesting theoretical framework that could address outstanding questions about the fundamental forces of nature.

All specific numbers and identities in conformal field theory require justification, which is precisely what ward relationships provide. Initially developed by Altschuler, Di Francesco, and Goujard, we are showing that their initial formula can be modified to obtain a more comprehensive formula incorporating multiple spin operators, thereby building on their initial findings.

We establish that Coxeter groups, whose defining graph has a finite diameter, possess a specific type of presentation known as a solution presentation, which arises from the fundamental property of being automatically equipped with a reliable decision-making procedure for pair membership.

An intriguing aspect of brain function is the relationship between walking and the human brain, a fundamental aspect of motor control that has been studied extensively. Despite the comprehension of underlying neural mechanisms and reconstructed walking movements from electrocorticogram signals by our robotic legs in previous research, the exact correlation between brain signals and walking state has yet to be determined. To address this gap, a novel approach was developed to map the correlation between walking states and step rates from electrocorticogram signals by utilizing support vector machines. The purpose of this approach is to serve as a foundation for decoding walking states and step rates, achieving accurate results according to our study. Specifically, state decoding yielded nearly perfect results, with an average accuracy of 98.37% above baseline levels. Furthermore, predicting step rates yielded promising results, with the proposed method outperforming baseline levels by 14.80% in our study. This research expands upon prior understanding of the walking movement's neural mechanisms by uncovering the complex interplay between brain signals, walking states, and step rates, a fundamental aspect that has significant implications for the development of robust and high-grade prosthetic legs.

If we take a right-angled Artin group $G$ and a partition of its vertex set into two non-empty parts, say $L$ and $R$, and assume that the subgroup controlled by the left part $L$ acts freely on the associated right-angled Artin complex $\Ka$, then we can obtain a free action of the right-angled Artin group controlled by the right part $R$ on a quotient space $\Ka/\Ka'$, where $\Ka'$ denotes the kernel of the projection map from $\Ka$ to the space associated with $R$. Conversely, given a free action of a right-angled Artin group $H$ on a space $X$, if we let $V_H$ denote the set of vertices controlled by $H$, and let $L$ and $R$ be two non-empty subsets of $V_H$ with $L \cup R = V_H$ and $L \cap R = \emptyset$, then the subgroups controlled by $L$ and $R$ act freely on $X$ if and only if the action of $H$ on $X$ induces isomorphic actions on the quotient spaces $X/ X_H'$ and $X/ X_H''$, where $X_H'$ and $X_H''$ are the kernels of the projection maps from $X$ to the spaces associated with $L$ and $R$ respectively.

Connectivity estimation in functional connectomics is critically influenced by several factors, and connectivity over time also plays a significant role.  However, analyzing long sequences of functional connectivity data can be challenging due to computational requirements and the need for large amounts of data.  Additionally, connectivity in the brain is not constant over time, changing significantly between different states such as wakefulness and sleep.  Current methods struggle to effectively capture temporal changes in connectivity reliably and efficiently.  A novel approach is proposed to overcome these challenges by using a combination of recurrent neural networks and graph neural networks to model time-dependent connectivity and provide a precise, compact representation of connectivity.  Simulation results demonstrate the superiority of this proposed method in terms of accuracy and efficiency, and a potential application to brain imaging is also presented.

Animals move through complex environments with ease, thanks to their innate ability to navigate and respond to dynamic environments.  Inspiring robotics designers and engineers, researchers have sought to quantify the underlying mechanics of biological motion, often relying on high-tech tools like motion capture and computed tomography.  Although these efforts have been focused on specific species such as insects and humans, with an eye to applying this knowledge to robotic design, the reverse perspective is also viable: using robotics to mimic biological movement could offer novel insights into the underlying computational principles governing biological motion.  From this dual perspective, the paper explores the reverse problem of extracting movement-related information from images of moving organisms, a challenging task that requires novel algorithms and techniques to reconstruct three-dimensional movement trajectories from two-dimensional image projections.  Through successful demonstrations involving both living subjects such as flying birds and artificially created objects, the paper shows that its approach to analyzing movement from limited, partially obscured image data can produce accurate and practical results, with far-reaching potential applications in fields like wildlife studies, sports analysis, and movie special effects.

The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear algebra problems, particularly those involving large matrices. To mitigate these difficulties, researchers have examined alternative methods for matrix inversion, such as the iterative application of the matrix's inverse. Building upon our prior work (reference 1), we have developed a novel approach to efficiently compute the inverse of a matrix via an iterative procedure that employs a third-order technique. This method leverages the matrix's inverse in a pairwise operation to achieve fast convergence. We have tested and evaluated our proposed approach, and the resulting algorithm has demonstrated superior performance when compared to naive methods for small-scale matrix inversion. Moreover, this algorithm can be readily integrated into GPU-accelerated environments.

The Topological Insulator phenomenon is characterized by a robust energy gap resulting from topological protection, which can be determined through the calculation of a Zak phase. To maintain this feature, TI materials require minimal fluctuations in their atomic structure. In contrast, matter that exhibits the Topological Anderson Conductivity (TAC) phenomenon shows no restriction on its atomic composition. A theoretical model based on a random binary disorder should help elucidate the underlying physics of TAC materials. Utilizing a tight-binding framework, we developed a 1D and 2D model with random placement of atoms from two different elements within a honeycomb lattice. The resulting phase diagram reveals unique indicators of the TAC phase, including a constant Zak phase or momentum-space polarization, which serve as immutable markers of the TAC state. Notably, the size of the energy gap fluctuates in direct proportion to the standard deviation of the disorder, which can be influenced by adjusting the hopping parameter. Our discovery of a universal standard deviation of the energy gap also occurs in 2D, albeit with a critical threshold. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that topological properties can be permanently maintained in materials with atomic composition fluctuations, thereby introducing a new class of materials known as Topological Anderson Conductors.

We introduce a theoretical model where cuts and morphisms work in unison to define a symbolic rewriting system. This framework, tailored for handling an infinite number of rules, provides a solid foundation for evaluating composite functions resulting from an infinite number of applications of these rules. Specifically, we demonstrate that both the Babbage and Reachability problems can be efficiently resolved using this framework, with efficient solutions to these problems implying, in turn, the undecidability of their respective decision-making counterparts.

We investigate the characteristics of Higgs boson production in the minimal supersymmetric standard model, considering complex parameters and focusing on on-shell Higgs physics. The development employs the SUSY-HIGGSDR package, which provides an analytical framework for calculating SUSY processes and is now expanded to include complex phases. The study delves into the decay and production of all individual Higgs bosons, incorporating corrections and corrections that emerge from the misalignment between the CP rest frame and the particle's momentum frame. The analysis yields over 1800 expressions for observable quantities, incorporating higher-order effects due to particle interactions and based on on-shell principles for calculational consistency.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses a decentralized, memoryless contextual linear bandit learning problem. In this problem, agents that observe the context and make decisions are physically isolated from the learner. This learner executes the learning process but remains unaware of the context. Contexts are assumed to be generated randomly and a new approach is presented. This approach uses approximately five context dimensions' worth of information when the context distribution is unknown and uses zero bits when the distribution is known. This approach offers nearly the same regret bound as if contexts were fully observable. This achievement is notable as it outperforms existing bounds by a significant margin. This achievement particularly occurred when the time horizon is substantial. When the distribution is known the approach offers an information theoretically optimal bound.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which provides a supernumerary comment. Regarding challenges in estimating (PTPR) with data sampling issues, we propose a simple estimator with two-steps. In the first step, we use inverse probability weighting to estimate PTPR, which yields an unbiased estimator. However, this estimator is not efficient due to the non-linear relationship between regression scores and the index function. We rectify this inefficiency by applying the efficient score estimator in the second step, which leads to the application of the inverse of the information matrix of the regression scores. In the process, we derive the explicit form of the information matrix of the regression scores, which is novel in itself. Notably, this form confirms the findings of Tewathas (2020) and Tewathas et al. (2020) under specific conditions. To extend the research to multiple instruments, we propose a alternative approach that employs the empirical influence function, which enables us to estimate the target parameter using the empirical influence function estimator. Interestingly, this estimator is identical to the regular estimator under quadratic loss. All additional proofs and details are provided in the supplementary material.

Our study introduces two new event shape variables, transverse momentum of the second-harmonic flow and transverse momentum of the most detached fragment, designed to manipulate collision outcomes and influence the measurement of elliptic flow. Calculating these variables for 2.76 TeV proton-proton and lead-lead collisions allows us to compare inclusive charged particle spectra in different collision regions. Ultimately, our findings indicate that variations in inclusive spectra are primarily influenced by the density of initial states rather than fluctuations in density. Moreover, our research facilitates an important understanding of elliptic flow measurements in lead-lead collisions, highlighting the significance of initial state properties and minimal dependence on final state particles.

This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses to examine the extremal GDoF differences resulting from optimal versus binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks. Under the assumption of a static environment and non-cooperative nodes, we first determine the extremal GDoF difference when there are $K$ users. Subsequently, we investigate dynamic scenarios in which the number of active users can change, and determine the conditions under which the extremal GDoF difference is proportional to $\sqrt{K}$. For both cases, lower and upper bounds for the extremal GDoF difference are established. In particular, the upper bounds are derived from the outcomes of a game theory analysis, while the lower bounds result from combining binary power control with a particular scheduling method. When the number of active users remains dynamic and can vary between any two numbers, we find that the extremal GDoF difference is proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ is the maximum possible number of active users.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration method utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our multiple-time-step integration method was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially lengthening collision time steps can lead to particles becoming too energetic, however, by reducing this bias, our method is more suitable for simulating complex scenarios involving numerous particles.

This article presents a novel approach to addressing a long-standing conjecture regarding the term $f(n)=a^n+b^n$ in the sequence 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 61, 124, 251, 512,... where all known roots can be found within the set of positive integers and are part of the solutions to at least one of the following equations: $a+b=2^k$, $ab=7^m$, or $f(n)\equiv 0 \mod n$.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of ground reaction forces as the terrain shifts and the subsequent impact on a robot's stability and movement. To better understand these complex interactions, a simplified simulation model was developed to accurately depict ground deformation caused by a hopping monopod's impact. By utilizing the discrete element method (DEM) within a multibody dynamics framework, the model successfully simulated various terrain compositions and surface interactions. To enhance the model's effectiveness for control system development, the team performed a comprehensive identification of the system's parameters and carried out simulations to assess the model's precision. The resulting model exhibits excellent agreement with actual measurements and provides a reliable platform for testing control systems and exploring legged locomotion on deformable ground.

In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to the study of meson form factors. Quark and meson wave functions' overlap integrals are determined and a set of general form factor formulas is derived. These formulas enable the calculation of a variety of meson form factors using a unified approach. As specific examples, the electric radii of $π$, $K$, and $D$ mesons are computed and contrasted with experimental data when available.

An organization's information typically requires a clear and efficient framework to effectively guide understanding and decision-making. As information systems grow in size and complexity, their underlying structures often necessitate a more nuanced and multi-faceted representation, involving interconnections and layered relationships. In such information networks, with nodes representing concepts and edges denoting relationships and connections, the automatic generation of hierarchical frameworks can provide a compressed and intuitive representation of complex data. This research explores the automatic creation of hierarchical frameworks from information networks and focuses on a novel method to broaden existing concepts into more general principles, incorporating empirical evaluations to compare the proposed approach against established methods.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system. Quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems. In contrast, quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to a system's Hamiltonian, resulting in non-equilibrium states that evolve over time. The distinction between these processes affects their suitability for addressing specific computational tasks. While quenching can lead to highly entertaining and complex temporal developments, quenching from an uncomputing phase inevitably gives rise to chaotic behavior in the time-evolving system, rendering it ineffective for solving difficult optimization problems. Consequently, researchers have established a minimum threshold for the duration of an annealing interval in order to avoid quench-like behavior and solve problems efficiently. This study investigates the relationship between the annealing interval and quenching-like behavior in the context of quantum annealing for the intricate cover problem.

We developed a two-dimensional model that incorporates strong interactions within a specific nickelate material. This model includes strong correlations affecting both nickel and oxygen atoms. Using a combination of numerical methods and analytical techniques, we investigated the screening of a localized hole by infinitesimal amounts of hole-like doping. This investigation focused on the implications for superconducting infinite-layer nickelate materials. A key finding shows that even minimal screening can significantly reduce the energy gap associated with the localized, charge-exclusion state. This effect can lead to an apparent decrease in the effective on-site Coulomb interaction. We discovered that the influence of screening varies based on the doping type and charge carrier composition. In particular, we found that small amounts of hole-like doping can lead to minimal screening of the localized site, whereas large amounts of electron-like doping result in more extensive screening. As such, we suggest that the self-doping mechanism plays a crucial role in infinite-layer nickelates. We investigate a quantum mechanical model where a microscopic degree of freedom, described by a bosonic operator, occupies a specific spatial region in the form of a compass shape. The analysis focuses on the operator's large system behavior as it operates on an infinite, one-dimensional background. The study calculates the expected value of various classical phase polarization operators in the compass state's Fock space, especially those related to the North, South, East, and West phases. The research reveals that the expected values of these operators correlate strongly, with their collective behavior influenced by the compass shape's asymmetry. The system's phase polarization's fluctuations are substantial and stem from the interplay between the confining potential's extremes. The calculation of the total phase polarization's variance yields a constant value equal to half the average total classical phase polarization. The research also examines the assembly's motion by calculating the expected values of position and momentum operators in the Fock space. The study finds that the assembly's motion is analogous to that of a harmonic oscillator when its mean position is at the center of the confining potential, whereas the momentum operator's expected value fluctuates between the minimum and maximum possible values.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI's generation of particles and settling could create a feedback loop, unless this phenomenon is considered, dust evolution models may be misinterpreted. In the outer regions of a protoplanetary disk, researchers found that the VSI's impact on particle growth and settling is minimal as entropy released during particle collisions is insufficient to prompt VSI, delaying the onset of VSI until about 0.5 AU in a typical solar-like system. As VSI enhances particle growth through settling, this finding suggests that particle growth in these areas may be slower than previously thought. Furthermore, by analyzing the VSI's effects on particle growth and settling, researchers found that even a weakened VSI would still result in accelerated particle growth, although this growth is curtailed once particles reach a certain size, depending on dust type. In the absence of an outward pressure force, VSI also exhibits an interesting propensity for particles 10 micrometers in size, settling more quickly in areas further from the central star.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established boundary regularity result from the literature. Consequently, this leads to an alternative proof of a previously established conjecture regarding the stability of a specific type of manifold maintained over time, and it also enables the integration of harmonic functions in this context.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning and pattern, thus enabling detection mechanisms to function effectively. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and ABS to be vulnerable to triggers that are dynamic, meaning they are unaffected by pattern or location, thus compromising their reliability. What is even more challenging, is that these sophisticated backdoors require an inordinate amount of compromised training data. In a breakthrough study, it has been found that even without significantly compromising training data, hidden functionalities could arise from the presence of a specific neural network structure called the global mean pooling layer, despite initial difficulty in accomplishing this feat in various machine learning tasks such as sound classification, text sentiment analysis, and image classification.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of parallax uncertainties were refined to mirror Gaia's observational modes and signal processing. Evaluating the permissible range of $\gamma$'s variation, we found this deviation to be directly proportional to the square of the uncertainty in $1/\gamma$. This led to a calculated uncertainty of 0.13 microarcseconds in parallax measurements, which could be improved with future measurements of $\gamma$.

To improve the performance of open-domain Commonsense Question Answering, 
we propose a novel approach that involves creating a set of simple, semi-
semi-supervised questions mirroring real question-answer pairs. These new
questions are designed to reflect the underlying semantics and relationships
between existing question-answer pairs, with no explicit supervision for 
the questions themselves. We leverage a pre-trained paragraph-level machine
learning model to extract semantic-related questions automatically, drawing 
from a vast amount of freely available text on the internet. To enhance the
quality of these generated questions, we employ a combination of human 
evaluation and selective human verification, incorporating only the most 
semantically meaningful questions into our dataset. The resulting Coarse-to-
Careful (C2C) dataset comprises 200,000 question-answer pairs across nine 
categories, with a focus on realistic difficulty levels similar to actual 
open-domain CQA systems. Comprehensive experiments using the C2C dataset 
indicate significant performance improvements for various strong BERT-based CQA 
models, particularly when they are trained on a combination of the original 
open-ended CQA dataset and our proposed C2C dataset.

Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular ions whose spectral patterns are not well understood. To advance the comprehension of these phenomena, research is being conducted to develop a comprehensive model of comet-like environments using a computational chemistry approach. As a significant step in this endeavor, a theoretical spectroscopic analysis of excited states for various oxygen-containing molecular ion combinations is being investigated. However, the existing research base shows a notable discrepancy in available data on some of these compounds, such as RCN, NCO, CO, CN, OCN, NO, NO+, FOF, OF, CF, CF+, CF2, COf, and CO2. A enhanced understanding of these molecules' spectral characteristics through computational simulations is being obtained, and the resulting data is being incorporated into a spectral library for possible matching with observational comet spectrum data.

In the context of a Parameter Disparity Framework, where data distributions vary significantly across individual contributors, addressing scalability and representation challenges becomes a superior approach to tackling large contributor pools. Given that contributors often participate in a federated learning process for only one session, typically with limited representation capacity, learning from heterogeneous data on a large scale is exceedingly difficult. In response to these challenges, we present the Stroll algorithm, a novel collaborative learning framework that leverages random walks to unite contributors with similar data distributions. By participating in the Stroll for just one session, contributors of any size can contribute effectively to a parameter estimation process that accurately represents the entire pool of contributors. Our theoretical and practical evaluations validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the Stroll algorithm under various conditions.

Individuals within the criminal justice system are undergoing mental health assessments, yet the Compulsory Treatment Order (CTO) that results from these tests, requiring individuals to undergo mental health treatment, has an untested impact on their mental health, as well as their chances of reoffending. To examine the unexplored effects of CTOs, researchers leveraged a unique dataset containing detailed information about convicted offenders, including their mental health, sentencing, and future reoffending and sentencing history. Using this data, researchers conducted an extensive set of tests to evaluate the CTO's impact on an individual's mental health, as well as their likelihood of committing a future nonviolent or violent crime. Interestingly, the analysis revealed that CTOs have a minimal impact on an individual's mental health but also discovered that such orders could increase an individual's chances of committing a future nonviolent crime. Nevertheless, CTOs were found to have no significant influence on an individual's likelihood of committing a violent crime. Moreover, the research uncovered that the likelihood of committing a future nonviolent crime could be Rawlsian-unfairly distributed, as it disproportionately affects marginalized populations, including those who are economically disadvantaged, have lower levels of education, or identify as Indigenous. Notably, the analysis demonstrated that the likelihood of committing a violent crime is equally unevenly distributed.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a new regularization technique that enhances the consistency of partially labeled images, leading to improved performance in semi-supervised medical image segmentation tasks. The proposed method leverages a modified version of the patchMatch cut-filling technique to fill undefined image regions based on annotated areas, and it incorporates a novel consistency loss function that penalizes differences between original and filled image patches. By strategically balancing the consistency loss and the standard cross-entropy loss, the method yields exemplary results on public datasets ABIDE (average Dice score: 0.856) and MMWHS (average Dice score: 0.831).

To measure the complexity of a dynamic system's microscale dynamics, we use a novel approach based on graph neural networks that incorporates time-dependent energy spectra. Utilizing this method, we determine the quantum entropy rate and fractal dimension of a one-dimensional chaotic map by numerically resolving its quantum dynamics over multiple iterations. Our approach yields a precise, time-independent assessment of the map's dimensional complexity, which we find to be identical to its Lyapunov exponent. To extend this analysis to a statistically chaotic scenario, we calculate the entropy rate and fractal dimension of a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator subject to a random force, which serves as a benchmark for our approach. Our results consist of an operational protocol for measuring the complexity of a chaotic system by mapping the entropy rate-fractal dimension plane, and are made accessible to the scientific community through an open-source coding framework.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by a single-parameter family of density functions. Assume that a sample of size $n$ is drawn from one of the density functions in this family, where the drawing process is random, occurring according to a mixture distribution with an unknown parameter $\tau$ that averages the density functions. The goal of this study is to estimate the parameter that defines the density function and the average parameter of the mixture distribution based on the maximum likelihood principle. However, since the sample contains information from multiple density functions, simply applying maximum likelihood estimation is insufficient. To address this challenge, we propose using the parameters of a second-order mixture distribution, whose density functions are determined by the density functions of the original mixture distribution and whose parameter $\tau$ is known or can be estimated. When the drawing process involves multiple layers of mixing, we can similarly use the parameters of a third-order mixture distribution, and so on. This general framework enables us to estimate the average of a set of density function parameters based on the maximum likelihood principle. To demonstrate the utility of this approach, we generate random samples from an exponential distribution with an unknown parameter $\theta$ using the discrete mixing distribution $F_\theta$, which leads to the estimation problem addressed by Joe (1985). Similarly, we generate random samples from the discrete mixing distribution $F_\theta$ to obtain the estimation problem addressed by Nawab and Pourchot (1988).

Knowledge tracing in online educational platforms is a emerging technology that aims to automatically identify a student's underlying knowledge structure based on their interactive data with a computer program. To evaluate the effectiveness of knowledge tracing models, researchers employ various metrics, including accuracy, F1-score, and expected gradient descent. However, these metrics do not account for the temporal relationships present in student interaction data. To address this challenge, a new evaluation framework is proposed that leverages the concept of session-based reinforcement learning to anticipate a student's correct answer on each interaction. This approach enables the simultaneous optimization of model accuracy and adherence to the temporal patterns in student interaction data. To facilitate collaborative knowledge tracing research, the code for this proposed method is made available to the public.

Given any real-analytic manifold $M$, we can demonstrate that linear elliptic differential operators on $M$ possess closed ranges. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it can be shown that these operators are invertible. This invertibility aspect also extends to the context of differential forms on compact manifolds that are free from compact components.

Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT's format for proof objects was introduced, aiming to accommodate various proof-based algorithms in SMT solvers. Since then, solvers like CVC4, SMT6, and Z3 have adopted this standard, making it a de facto standard in the community. VeriT's development continued, refining its approach to handle a broad spectrum of problems efficiently. Now, with an optimized theory solver and a more sophisticated decision procedure, VeriT successfully participates in the SAT competition. Its participation is made possible by converting SAT problems into SAT, thanks to a new feature called "incremental rewriting." This technique enables dynamic theory extensions and rewriting rules during problem solving. Solving techniques like recursive decomposition and real quotient are also new capabilities of the VeriT solver.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The asynchronous approach, which allows updates to be sent at any time, addresses this issue but may lead to difficulties in ensuring the stability of the aggregated model. The proposed Unrestricted Federated Learning (UFL) framework relaxes the requirement that gradients must be recent, enabling the development of robust models even with delayed updates. To overcome the challenge of large effective learning rate, UFL uses a buffered asynchronous aggregation method that maintains stability while still allowing asynchronous updates. In UFL, each device can choose an arbitrary interval between updates, resulting in the development of robust models that are comparable to those obtained with synchronized learning. Experimental results on datasets with a wide range of sizes show that UFL outperforms synchronized learning and often matches the accuracy of asynchronous learning with careful hyperparameter tuning.

To enhance end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems for low-resource languages, a proposed approach leverages high-quality speech recognition models from a related high-resource language. The method involves two key steps: refining the low-resource language's phonetic representation using a style transfer technique to match the related high-resource language's representation; and training a multilingual ASR model on the related high-resource language's data, with a transfer learning component for the low-resource language. The proposed approach is tested on four low-resource languages using Welsh and English as reference languages, and the results show that ASR models trained on a single high-quality model for the related high-resource language outperform those trained on a multilingual model without transfer learning. Moreover, the study examines various style transfer techniques and phonetic representations to determine the optimal methods for three of the low-resource languages.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating through unfamiliar environments.  By leveraging Gaussian process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate scalable online predictions, we implement a block-structured inverse, and to prevent Gaussian process regression growth during TD updates, we develop a targeted target update strategy.  Our algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through successful, collision-free navigation in two complex, dynamically generated ocean scenarios.  Our results show that our algorithm excels at high speeds and extensive environment exploration, and surpasses a traditional TD learning approach and a semi-parametric TD learning approach in several key metrics.

We employ a sophisticated anisotropic dual-fluid model to examine relativistic stellar objects with distinct components, such as neutron stars and strange quark stars. This approach allows us to derive the mass-radius relationship for specific interactions, including electromagnetic and scalar interactions. Our results show that the mass-radius relationship in our model aligns with corresponding results from the literature, demonstrating that the anisotropic dual-fluid model accurately replicates anisotropic single-fluid models. Furthermore, we investigate how the presence of a dense quark star component affects the mass-radius relationship of neutron stars. Our findings indicate that the mass-radius relationship of neutron stars remains unchanged when the quark star component occupies a minimal fraction of the total mass. However, when the quark star component dominates the mass, we observe two possible scenarios: (1) a sudden shift in the mass-radius relationship at a critical mass, or (2) an continuous transition from a neutron star to a quark star, depending on the specific equation of state.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, few-shot domain adaptation tasks are underexplore. We examine whether meta-learning can be applied to GEC. The results show that using metadata alone yields similar or often better performance than pseudo data, and utilizing both metadata and pseudo data leads to a significant improvement over both individual approaches. We discovered that using a student-teacher model leads to a small gain. The most notable finding is that the performance of both the teacher and student models stabilizes quickly as we add more support examples in few-shot domain adaptation tasks. The code and model are available at the following link: https://github.com/ghrua/FSDT-GEC.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our analysis, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the input, always produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared values as input. Building on a prior study by Mei and Yu, we demonstrate the existence of efficient and envy-free mechanisms in a wide range of valuation settings, where all possible equilibria correspond to fair allocations resulting from these mechanisms. Furthermore, we establish that there is an inherent boundary to the level of fairness that can be achieved as the number of involved agents increases. Specifically, we prove that under general valuation settings, the minimum possible envy and the maximum possible efficiency in equilibria both converge to zero as the number of agents approaches infinity.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of positive and negative pion charges is conducted by computing two-current projections. The study yields a detailed understanding of how pion charges behave in different two-current combinations, thereby providing valuable insights for momentum operators in nucleon effective field theories, particularly in the context of chiral effective field theories, where the role of two-current combinations in defining the isoscalar-scalar charge is particularly relevant.

Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
However, accurately using observed relations in this context is hampered by
not properly accounting for variations in mass accretion rates, a problem
especially prevalent in earlier stages of star formation. Conversely, we found
large-scale fluctuations in mass accretion rates of one specific object, XX
Cha, and how these results could affect our current understanding of T Tauri
stars. Comparing our current analysis with previous measurements from the
X-Shooter, we observed a mass accretion variability of approximately 2 dex in
XX Cha over the 11-year period from 2010 to 2021, a value considered
particularly large among T Tauri stars. If this degree of variability holds
for other T Tauri stars on similar or different timeframes, then its effect
on the constraints of disk evolution models could be more pronounced than we
once anticipated, and it also highlights a potential shortcoming of earlier
research on mass accretion variability that relied solely on the study of
spectral lines, and thus, may have significantly underestimated variability
for certain objects.

Offline Model-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARMALD) models latent dynamics and interactions between agents and can be effective for a wide range of collaborative tasks. However, training such models using only observed data from multiple interacting agents is challenging due to the large action spaces, partial observations, and difficulty in estimating the underlying dynamics. To address this, we present a novel method, called Learning from Good Paths (LGP), that selectively uses effective agent policies to transfer knowledge to the model, enabling it to capture essential aspects of the environment and interactions. As a result, LGP is suitable for complex, unseen environments with varying numbers of agents. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on multiple benchmarks, showing significant improvements over existing offline model-based multi-agent learning methods.

We developed a novel approach to align MV images obtained from two different depths. The proposed method involves using a Convolutional Neural Network to detect corresponding organs between images, with a subsequent refinement using a non-rigid registration technique to account for variations in soft tissues. This method's performance was evaluated using synthetic data with realistic noise levels and actual patient images, yielding promising results for both training and validation datasets. The proposed technique was compared to a state-of-the-art registration method using a figure-of-merit function based on patient image segmentation, with a significant improvement observed in alignment quality. Additionally, we investigated the feasibility of aligning images obtained from different depths, with encouraging results presented.

When examining the fundamental characteristics of quantum states and their associated operations, single-particle entanglement has been subject to both positive and negative interpretations. On one hand, it's seen as a local resource that generates non-local effects through the action of quantum operations. On the other hand, some argue it lacks genuine non-local properties, instead behaving similarly to classical correlations in certain contexts. This paper disputes the second viewpoint by demonstrating a genuinely non-local effect - namely, the true extent of the non-locality in a certain scenario that involves single-particle entanglement. This specific example involves a joint measurement that leads to the appearance of non-local effects on one particle alone, depending on the action performed on the other. This effect manifests as a genuine non-locality even when the state in question is highly mixed. Notably, this effect isn't found in unentangled states, indicating it's a distinctive indicator of single-particle entanglement. Moreover, by restricting the types of allowed operations, we can delve deeper into the non-local properties of entangled states, thereby gaining a more precise understanding of the relationship between non-locality and the generation of entanglement.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has led to a higher risk of cyber attacks, especially targetable and privacy-related issues.  In response to these challenges, there has been a growing interest in Federated Learning (FL) and its application to IoVs.  However, the current research in FL IoV focuses mainly on optimizing algorithm efficiency and reducing latency and does not sufficiently address the privacy-related challenges.  To address this limitation, a new literature review is conducted on Blockchain-based FL for IoVs, known as BFL-FL IoV.  This new framework combines the benefits of FL and Blockchain technology to address the privacy concerns and security risks in IoVs.  Through an analysis of eight notable BFL-FL IoV protocols, this review highlights the integration of FL with Blockchain technology as a viable solution to address the security and privacy challenges in IoVs.  It also outlines potential research directions and calls for further study on the BFL-FL IoV framework.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly three and a half days while the absence of the white dwarf spin frequency presents further evidence for a massive WD.  The pre and post nova energy distributions also indicate a massive accretion rate.  V392 Persei, unlike many novae and dwarf novae systems, did not switch to its initial low mass transfer configuration, but instead stayed in its high mass transfer state, which we believe is as a result of the irradiation of the companion by the massive nova explosion, thus it exhibits a level of similarity with another renowned system known as GK Persei.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to reduce transmission delays and improve performance. Initially, a limited number of GMM components are created to serve as the precoder codebook entries. To minimize the distortion between learned GMM components and actual precoders, a criterion is designed to guide the feedback encoding process. During operation, the receiver measures the distortion between GMM components and precoders, but only feeds back the indices of the most similar components. This approach reduces feedback data volume but introduces additional distortion. To manage this extra distortion, a new criterion is defined to influence the feedback encoding process. Further enhancements are achieved by selecting a subset of GMM components based on anticipated precoders, thereby reducing the feedback volume and enhancing performance. Numerical examples demonstrate the proposed system's performance advantages.

A type of strong, steady-state current that flows through a one-dimensional chain has been lacking. Researchers have demonstrated that this kind of current can arise from periodic driving and spin-chain cryptography. However, achieving a similar strong, steady-state current in three-dimensional lattices has proven challenging. A specific non-equilibrium setup, involving a Hofstadter model and based on the Kitaev quantum annealing protocol, is shown to produce robust, light-speed surface currents flowing in predictable directions, even when driven far from equilibrium. This effect is highly sensitive to dimensionality and cannot be replicated in two-dimensional or one-dimensional lattices. Moreover, this phenomenon allows for robust quantum state transfer, as evidenced by transferring a spin-1/2 state from a three-dimensional Hofstadter model to a distant site along its surface, using only surface currents and no direct interaction.

Reimers formulated an important relation to calculate stellar mass loss, but it is necessary to incorporate a correction factor to accurately determine mass loss rates. This study modifies Reimers' formula by replacing the total luminosity with the intrinsic luminosity, yielding a more precise mass loss estimate. Evaluating this modified relation for a range of main sequence stars, we find that it effectively limits maximum mass loss rates and supports the notion that there is a fundamental boundary beyond which certain stars cannot form due to mass loss.

We examine the likelihood of low-mass white dwarfs and neutron stars formed from the remains of the first stars in nuclear star clusters at the centers of galaxies. These dense remnant stars can merge and produce gravitational waves. Calculating the number of such mergers, we find that most occur in the nuclei of large spiral galaxies rather than globular clusters. Using simulations of galaxy evolution and relativistic dynamics, we estimate the number of detectable gravitational waves from these events by the Square Kilometre Array era. Specifically, we find that the number of gravitational waves from white dwarf mergers in the remains of the first stars in nuclear star clusters is in the order of $N_{\rm WD} \approx 2.5-13.8$ and for pulsar mergers in the order of $N_{\rm PS} \approx 0.06-0.85$. These estimates are also compared to other possible sources of gravitational waves from the early universe.

In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests involving thousands of text-based actions and a more realistic training data sets.
Our findings show that by greatly accelerating the simulation environment, we can significantly boost the effectiveness of training virtual agents by enabling the use of more advanced training methods that were previously impractical due to speed constraints.

Deep learning models, particularly those using recurrent neural networks, have found extensive applications in various tasks by leveraging large amounts of data. However, the computational complexity of these models hinders their practical implementation on limited-resource devices. To overcome this constraint, we propose an energy-efficient LSTM architecture that combines low-precision computation and a hierarchical memory module. To minimize power consumption while maintaining performance, we designed a compact LSTM structure with reduced hidden dimensions and optimized learning rates. The complementary memory module stores frequently accessed data in a smaller, more accessible section. We validated our approach using video identification datasets and achieved comparable results with traditional LSTM networks while reducing computational complexity by up to 83%.

In a type of quantum field theory known as conformal field theories, a set of complex numbers is correlated in a specific way that determines the shapes of bound objects. When a positive charge is added to these correlations, the resulting numbers maintain their convexity, a property that is not generally preserved when the charge is replaced by a combination of charges. Convexity is observed in a broad range of field theories, but it is not a fundamental principle and may be broken by certain combinations of charges. If convexity were to disappear in a way that could be detected with high-energy particles, it might indicate the presence of a type of gravitational force that shapes the world around it. While the accuracy of this prediction has not been thoroughly verified, it has been found to hold in a limited group of field theories that include some with and without reference to the principles of general relativity.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific property called F-regularity, we establish an equivalent condition in terms of a specific ring theoretic concept called tight Hilbert function. This condition also appears in a different form that involves polynomial equations and system of parameters. Furthermore, this relationship leads to a specific formula that computes the dimension of such a ring.

Public sector organizations often purchase services from independent contractors to accomplish specific tasks.
