This practice affects how markets and services evolve, yet the underlying dynamics of these interactions are not well understood.  To address this limitation, a new model is developed that considers multiple interacting markets and reveals how policy changes affect service availability and pricing.  The proposed framework is applicable to various applications, including healthcare, transportation, and energy, and helps policymakers anticipate the consequences of their actions on these complex systems.

We investigate prime factors of numbers in integer polynomial sequences. If a polynomial generates a prime-producing sequence, we show its factors must divide the initial term. Conversely, if all its factors divide the first term, this condition is sufficient to ensure the sequence contains only prime numbers, except for 2 and 3, produced by simple quadratic equations.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The entire phenomenon was obscured by the strong north polar stratospheric jet that developed in the late 1990s and has persisted ever since. The strong jet prevents observations of the summertime polar vortex in the northern hemisphere. The vortex typically forms in the lower atmosphere and gradually warms the upper atmosphere over the course of a few years. The exclusion of the northern hemisphere's summer vortex from the record of previous observations is due to the persistent stratospheric jet that developed in the late 1990s. The presence of the vortex is inferred from analyses of the distribution of the atmospheric compound argon-38, which indicates that the entire stratospheric jet will disappear within the next few years, allowing for the direct observation of the summertime polar vortex in the northern hemisphere.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under nonlinear conditions outside a compact convex obstacle where solutions have a controlled growth. It is observed that for a class of convex objects and certain nonlinearity functions with critical strength, explosive solutions exist and are uniquely determined. Furthermore, when the nonlinearity is below the critical threshold, we find solutions for any convex shape. The research also reveals that small modifications of the linear Schrödinger equation with added nonlinearity near a compact, singular point can significantly alter solution behavior.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

We create a linearization functor for full linearization that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis defines the image of the full linearization functor, resulting in a subcategory of k-fold vector bundles. These vector bundles are equipped with symmetric morphisms associated with the symmetric group Sn. A significant observation arises in the degree 2 scenario, where this added structure leads to the concept of symplectic double vector bundles. These have an opposite relationship with metric double vector bundles. The process of full linearization is also used to extend N-manifolds and a superising method for a graded bundle.

This research focuses on providing an appropriate framework for calculating certain orbital integrals, which are crucial in number theory and algebraic geometry. Specifically, we develop a method to compute the values of certain integral functions over algebraic groups by drawing on techniques from measure theory and algebraic geometry. This approach also enables us to examine the convergence of a specific sequence of measures, which is implicitly related to the arithmetic properties of specific algebraic entities. In the process, we establish a connection between the measures arising from integrating over group orbits and the measures associated with specific polynomial functions, which allows us to compare the measures of specific subsets of algebraic groups. Ultimately, this comparison helps us determine the density of certain subsets of groups relative to groups of the same dimension, which is a significant outcome in its own right.

The success of retrieved stage information from scanning tunneling microscopy (RTI-SNM) and spectroscopy (RTI-SSM) depends heavily on good signal-to-noise ratio and consistent scanning patterns. Although these requirements are generally met in static samples through slow surface scans, they can be challenging to achieve during dynamic measurements that involve rapid atomic movements. In this work, we demonstrate the application of RTI-SSM to identify atomic arrangements in irradiated atomic layers by analyzing scattered x-rays off excited electrons. This method allows for rapid stage inference across large areas, as well as through thick samples, and we showcase its capabilities using thin silver films and compare its validity with traditional analysis methods.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element method for single-phase Darcy flow within a media that contains a small number of prominent fractures. These fractures are represented as thin interfaces within which fluid moves according to a different, specified model of behavior. By employing a dual porosity representation and combining it with a hybrid-mixed finite element discretization, we develop a computational model capable of accurately capturing the effects of fractures on the flow dynamics. Unlike other mixed finite element formulations, this method avoids significant computational cost associated with solving fully coupled and nonlinear discrete systems. Instead, we derive a linearly solvable formulation for the fracture interfaces, and another for the porous matrix, which can be easily solved for the fluxes within that domain. We validate the effectiveness of this method through a series of numerical experiments, including those featuring non-linear friction within the fractures, and show it to be a robust and accurate approach for assessing the impact of fractures on flow dynamics within such complex media.

High-dimensional Bayesian methods can be extremely effective for model selection tasks by providing a objective score such as the Bayes factor. However, Bayes factors are highly sensitive to model drift due to their reliance on the absolute difference in log-likelihood scores. This issue can be mitigated by using the marginal likelihood, which is more robust to model drift but generally requires a significantly longer computation time. We examine two workflow strategies for reducing Bayes factor sensitivity while still utilizing Bayes factors. Firstly, we set $m-1$ models to zero variance and fix their parameters, finding this results in a small reduction in accuracy but a significant improvement in computational efficiency. Secondly, we explore clipping Bayes factors, discovering that clipping at a log-likelihood ratio of 10 yields the best balance between sensitivity and specificity. Our findings are consistently demonstrated across both linear regression and logistic regression models.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to analyze the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use.

We conduct a comprehensive landscape analysis of the nonconvex matrix decomposition problem under a new geometric framework, which allows us to create a precise map of the problem's landscape across all possible matrix rank values. We start by converting the matrix decomposition problem into an equivalent form that involves minimizing a quadratic function with respect to matrix variables, subject to an orthogonality constraint. This transformation enables us to perform our landscape analysis within the context of quaternions. Next, we establish that the geometric space associated with this problem is piecewise smooth and contains isolated singularities. Additionally, we identify specific regions of the geometric space that correlate with unique solution behaviors, including points corresponding to the minimum-rank solution, the all-zeros solution, and solutions with intermediate ranks. Notably, the isolated singularities are reframed as points of positive curvature that arise from the embedding of the Grassmannian manifold within the quaternions. This discovery demonstrates that the geodesic convexity of the matrix decomposition problem is equivalent to its positive definite curvature, thereby extending the existing results from convex matrix optimization to the nonconvex setting under a broader curvature criterion.

A graph is considered robust if it can be colored using a specific number of colors, denoted as $χ_, and any edge coloration containing at most $χ_- 1$ correctly colored edges will still be distinguishable from any permutation of the remaining unsolved edges.  This concept was first introduced by Brightwell and Winkler in 1996 as part of their work on counting the number of proper edge colorings of a given graph.  We are interested in exploring the relationship between a graph's robust edge coloring property and its underlying structure.  In particular, we aim to investigate if all cubic bipartite graphs require the same minimum number of colors to robustly color their edges.  To address this question, we need to examine if all cubic bipartite graphs share the same maximum distinction number, denoted as $d_B$.  Our contribution is a counterexample that illustrates which of these two conditions is actually more demanding.  We show that there are cubic bipartite graphs with a maximum distinction number of 4, thereby not all cubic bipartite graphs require the same minimum number of colors to robustly color their edges.  This counterexample also implies that all cubic bipartite graphs cannot all have the same maximum number of distinct edge colorations, making it necessary to introduce a broader classification that groups them together.

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of the Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation experiments, we validated the effectiveness of the social-learning approaches and examined several game dynamics. Additionally, we analyzed delays in learning and discovery of the NE, as well as the impact of population sizes in our simulations. My thesis is to explore the application of these methods to asymmetric Cournot games.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish that the symbolic and typical power lengths of $I(\mathcal{D})$ are equivalent, with specific values in the case of a oriented cycle. Moreover, the typical and symbolic second power lengths of $I(\mathcal{D})$ are also found to be the same, with a determination of this common value for a directed tree.

Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary floating point system. We also explore non-uniform data restriction techniques that efficiently minimize silent errors and hardware-induced data corruptions. The practical viability of this approach is shown through a vehicle classification test, using the ResNet-50 architecture and the CIFAR-10 dataset, pre-trained on a vast image database. The development of a practical safety case for this scenario is discussed, along with the implications for future low-error-rate detection methods.

Building upon the Jordanian twist framework, we derive a generalized version with an arbitrary parameter. This involves modifying the basic Jordanian twist and detailed exponential formulas for a 1-parameter subset of the BCK Lie algebra.

Our proposed CSEW model leverages the benefits of both monolingual and multi-lingual word embedding methods to create a unified framework that incorporates cluster information for enhanced performance. In this approach, we utilize both intra- and inter-lingual distributions to define the cluster-consistent word embedding equation, which we solve using a novel alternating least squares algorithm. Our experiments demonstrate improved clustering results, with the multi-lingual CSEW model outperforming the monolingual and multi-lingual baselines for both supervised and unsupervised clustering tasks. Moreover, the multi-lingual CSEW model excels in the semantic similarity evaluation, offering a competitive alternative to the multi-lingual MSM method.

The first paper in this series used 1.9 microbarn-negative free proton-nucleus interactions at the LHC. However, due to limited statistics, this study did not account for kaons. Consequently, this study combined 0.7 microbarn-proton-proton interactions at 7 TeV with 1.9 microbarn Xe-Pb interactions at 5.44 TeV to produce a comprehensive set of proton-proton, proton-kaon, and kaon-kaon interactions. Nonetheless, even with this combined sample size, the production of neutral kaons in Xe-Pe interactions remained undetected. Furthermore, due to limited statistics and similar masses, the results for meson and baryon interactions were found to be indistinguishable. Additionally, the results for the $\phi$-meson were found to agree with previous findings from the ALICE collaboration, which observed the $\phi$-meson in Pb-Pb collisions at the same center-of-mass energy.

This study uses a non-local Susceptible-Exposed-Infected (SEI) model to analyze the 2019 Chilean protests, which experienced varying levels of pandemic-related restrictions due to the proximity of the Torre Jojo, a central gathering spot in Santiago, and differing responses to protest-related infection risks. A unique aspect of this research lies in its non-local approach, as we account for the spread of infections beyond immediate neighborhoods. This method allows for the incorporation of mobility patterns resulting from the protests. A key component of the model incorporates discrete time periods, mirroring the scheduling of protests during weekends and weekdays. Numerical analysis of the model reveals that even with intense social gathering, the peak infection rates occur during weekday evenings, a finding that aligns with existing research. Conversely, existing non-local models fail to accurately capture the heightened infection rates within the Torre Jojo area during the weekends.

This research develops an innovative method for resolving constraints expressed as regular expressions with syntactic and semantic flaws, drawing on regular expression solving and rewriting techniques. Unlike traditional approaches, this method addresses issues with defined operators and identifies unmatched patterns. We apply this method to solve constraints within regular languages, establishing its soundness and completeness. Furthermore, this leads to a decision-making capability for whether two regular languages intersect or not.

We introduce a novel Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) approach, combining a deep neural network with an external memory attention mechanism to enhance mobility localization. Our VIO architecture, dubbed EMA-VIO, leverages both visual and inertial sensors to achieve robust and accurate positioning in a variety of mobility scenarios. We employ an external memory structure to store map points and associate them with visual-inertial features, using an attention-based mechanism to selectively compare only relevant map points to incoming visual-inertial tracking features. This allows for the efficient reduction of map sizes while comparing them to incoming data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of EMA-VIO by achieving the lowest localization error among all VIO-only participants in the VIO benchmark dataset for both the VIO and joint Visual-Inertial Localization (VIL) tasks, and surpass the accuracy of traditional VIO methods in various mobility scenarios.

A new theoretical framework based on the Weil matrix formalism has been developed to advance the understanding of non-linear electronic and photonic phenomena in exotic materials. This approach, in combination with rigorous mathematical proof, demonstrates that a unique class of materials, which we call higher-order Weyl materials with a square root symmetry, exhibit distinct non-linear optical properties in the long-wavelength limit. These materials display distinctive double-Weyl salient features that distinguish them from conventional higher-order Weyl materials and exhibit large non-linear photoconductivity and a specific non-linear photoconductivity spectrum consisting of a narrow band in the long-wavelength limit. These predictions can be experimentally verified through precise resistivity and optical conductivity measurements, providing a clear path to identifying a groundbreaking class of materials with unprecedented non-linear responses to light.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a linear inverse problem consisting of determining a time-varying current within a conductive medium using incomplete measurements of the electric field outside the medium, and we develop a numerical strategy to solve this problem.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Collection (FEDSEL) problem, a new approach to assembling global knowledge from disparate sources, where each contributor retains exclusive control over their information and chooses whether to contribute part of their data to the pool. We establish upper and lower bounds on the optimal solution for FEDSEL, and experimentally verify that selective contribution significantly enhances the effectiveness of traditional federated learning methods. Additionally, we find that contributors with diverse amounts of relevant information exhibit mixed behavior in a collaborative setting. To address this, we develop a straightforward yet impactful technique called Relevant-Enough-for-Selection (RES), where each contributor determines an individual threshold of sufficient information, and contribute accordingly. Consequently, contributors with ample relevant information tend to contribute less, which, when combined with selective contribution, enhances learning outcomes. Experimental evaluations using real and synthetic data demonstrate the superiority of RES over uniform threshold-based approaches.

We analyze the rank of elliptic curves in quartic extensions of the rationals, focusing on cases where the discriminant has Galois group $S_4$ or $A_4$. Notably, under both galois assumptions, there are instances where the rank of an elliptic curve increases compared to its rank over the rationals. Moreover, in cases with $S_4$ galois theory, we find examples of rank-one elliptic curves whose quartic extensions have rank two or greater. This achieves the objective of finding quartic extensions with a specific rank-increase condition initially proposed by Jean-Paul Tignol.

A variety of specifications must be met in order for a quantum system's entanglement to grow at a certain rate as it evolves over time. These requirements are reflected in the strong subadditivity of the von Neumann entropy and the quantum null energy condition entropy bound. When applied to a quasiperiodic scalar field in a one-plus-two-dimensional spacetime setting, these conditions yield different constraints on the field's average value and fluctuations. In particular, we find that the conditions for growth are met if the field's initial state has a specific form, and we also investigate the corresponding bounds on the rate of change of the system's entanglement with its own future null cone. Additionally, we determine the entanglement density and pressure of the field, as well as its total energy and pressure within a specific spatial interval, which can be seen as a type of quantum version of Tolman's law.

We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit to evolve from an arbitrary initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we establish a lower bound on which distinguishes the initial and final states for all possible measurement angles, and demonstrate that this duration can be achieved with a specific Hamiltonian. For non-unitary dynamics, induced by a combination of decoherence and transmission, we establish an upper bound on which depends on the initial and final states, as well as the rate of decoherence. A particular example of non-unitary dynamics, characterized by a collapse operator, is also analyzed. We connect these results to the Asymptotic Distinguishability Duration, and provide explicit expressions for both unitary and non-unitary cases. Furthermore, we derive upper bounds on the average asymptotic distinguishability duration for both unitary and non-unitary dynamics.

Let $X$, $Y$ be complex normed spaces and $Z$ a subspace of $X$ sharing the same topological characteristics. Assuming $X$ is uniformly convex, we establish that the norm of the classical interpolation operator from the space of absolutely continuous functions to the space of Holder continuous functions is equivalent to a specific constant.

A key limitation of superconducting quantum circuits is the poor understanding of their surface loss. To address this, we used terahertz scanning near-field microscopy to spatially map the dielectric breakdown and surface loss of resonators. Our findings show that lossy materials accumulate in areas around the microwave electrode due to dielectric disruption, leading to to the generation of defects that cause loss. By removing these defects during the etching process, we significantly reduced the surface loss, which was quantitatively verified through measurements of the resonators. Our cost-effective method of transferring the microwave patterns to the lossy materials using a helium ion beam also demonstrated minimal loss. Our research facilitates the development of high-fidelity quantum processors by providing practical guidelines for optimizing the design of quantum circuits.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future.

Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields.  Models like the nonlinear Hawkes process with multiple targets are commonly used to analyze these processes and their interactions, despite there being limited methods to estimate its parameters confidently.  We filled this gap by developing an initial Bayesian estimation method for the parameters of a Hawkes process with nonlinearity, as well as a variant with different targets, including a discussion on model selection.  Our approach involves using the mean squared error as a measure of estimation accuracy and conducting extensive simulations to compare its performance.  Additionally, we applied this method to real-world data sets consisting of online message boards and neuronal activity.

As high-power laser pulse interactions with matter become increasingly intense, the limitations of traditional linear polarization restrictions need to be addressed. We investigate the dynamic behavior of strong laser pulse polarization in intense interactions with a highly charged electron layer within a magnetized plasma. Our findings reveal that in extremely intense interactions, the polarization of the laser pulse can change instantly, affecting the pulse's intensity. This transformation can either enhance the original linear polarization to a degree that surpasses the initial intensity or switch the polarization to a circular or circularly enriched state. This sudden change in polarization occurs in both ultra-short and long laser pulses. Notably, as the electron layer's charge increases, the polarization alteration becomes more intense, influencing the pulse's dynamics and leading to the formation of a reflected circularly polarized pulse that can drive particle acceleration in a narrow, focused area.

Re-examining the parameters of the Standard Model through precise measurements of electroweak processes is highly sensitive to the magnitude of the tau lepton's electric dipole moment. As a tiny vector-like quantity, the tau's electric dipole moment can be a significant source of asymmetry in certain particle decay processes. Utilizing existing data and incorporating new insights into theoretical predictions, we have updated the estimate for the tau's electric dipole moment to as small as $4.2 \times 10^{-19}$ e cm, which is comparable to the magnitude of the neutrinoless quantum fluctuation in electron-positron interactions. Furthermore, we have explored the potential for future experiments to detect the tau's electric dipole moment at the Large Hadron Collider and Higgs factory.

We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we renew focus on spinning conformal field theory's operator product expansion (CFT OPE). In particular, we examine how CFT OPE blocks relate to conformal field theory's stress-energy tensor and its derivatives. Furthermore, we explore the AdS$_3$ stress-energy tensor within a specific conformal field theory context, generating a distinct set of spinning AdS$_2$ holographic blocks in two-dimensional CFT. Notably, our approach allows for the incorporation of massive spinning fields in AdS$_3$ holography.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson formulated a combinatorial approach to defining Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We provide evidence for the uniqueness of this formulation by proving it satisfies the same differentiability properties, thereby aligning it with the underlying mathematical framework in which Pontrjagin classes are typically used.

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases.

The effectiveness of lobster-eye optics in wide-field X-ray monitoring can be enhanced by utilizing a multi-unit configuration, our research indicates. Through simulations and tests, we found that for a 2x2 array of optics with 2deg field view per unit, the detection efficiency remains near 100% for a source scanning rate of 2deg per hour. Additionally, this configuration can facilitate the simultaneous monitoring of a large sky area, specifically 0.08steradians in 2deg field views, without significant reductions in detection sensitivity. These improvements can be maintained with the current technical capabilities of wide-field X-ray monitoring systems.

We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations.

To explore the interconnection between dark matter, gas, and stars in the early universe, we used a neural network to analyze a cosmic simulation and determined how the distribution of dark matter halos is affected by a key variable called the cosmic speed field. Based on an extensive database of simulated halos, we developed a sophisticated neural network to predict the properties of halos and found that the cosmic speed field influences the formation of halos over a wide range of masses, with a significant impact on their central parts. Specifically, we found that in areas with high cosmic speeds, halos tend to have smaller masses, particularly in the center, and that this effect is more pronounced in regions with certain physical characteristics, such as high densities of gas and stars. Furthermore, we found that the cosmic speed field exaggerates the existing problems halos already tend to have, rather than causing new issues, and that its effect on halos is similar to what would be expected from a well-established theoretical framework, with the exception of very large halos, where it behaves differently.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically extract data from complex documents lies in manually labeling large amounts of training data.  To address this issue, a new approach has been explored where only a small set of labeled documents, specifically those with unique layouts, are needed to train a versatile text parser.  This parser is capable of identifying the structure of most documents, even those with unfamiliar layouts.  Comprehensive testing has demonstrated that this approach is effective, surpassing the performance of existing methods even when only 10 labeled documents are utilized.  To facilitate the use of this approach in practical applications, a utility has been developed that can automatically parse documents across three different formats.  It is crucial to note that the existing models' permission to reproduce and distribute documents is assumed, and if this permission is not held, users are advised to obtain it from the relevant copyright holders.

The collaborations of advanced gravitational waves detectors like LIGO and Virgo obtain a vast stream of raw data from which signals from merging neutron star-black hole mergers need to be extracted. These collaborations rely heavily on sophisticated matched filtering techniques to match signal templates to the collected data, but this method is hindered by the limited computational power available. A breakthrough in this area comes from training convolutional neural networks on gravitational wave signals to classify signals from neutron star-black hole mergers, allowing for the efficient analysis of large datasets. This method achieves a high success rate in distinguishing real signals from noise and accurately identifies the mass ratio of the merged objects. Furthermore, a novel technique is introduced to recover the mass ratio using the output of the neural network, leading to a unified framework for recovering the mass ratio and distinguishing real signals from noise. This framework is utilized to analyze a large dataset of simulated signals from neutron star-black hole mergers, yielding a recovery rate of over 90% for often encountered mergers and providing a viable alternative to traditional matched filtering methods.

Urban settings benefit from physical diversity in their social encounters, which can be measured by the range of different incomes people interact with. During the COVID-19 pandemic, individuals altered their behavior to minimize pandemic risk, which took the form of increased home isolation and reduced participation in public activities. In response to these changes, urban settings saw a significant decline in face-to-face interactions among people in public spaces. Utilizing a unique dataset from Tokyo with both precise geographic and individual income data, this research documents the pandemic's effects on urban diversity in social encounters. It shows that income diversity in urban settings declined more rapidly in areas with higher population densities. In areas with the most dense populations, the pandemic reduced diversity in urban encounters by up to 12%. This research also examines various altered behaviors during the pandemic and finds that they all contributed to this decline in diversity, although to different degrees. Notably, areas with higher population densities experienced fewer new infections, suggesting that reduced social interaction may have some benefits in controlling the spread of the virus. However, public health policy priorities should weigh these benefits against the pandemic's adverse effects on urban diversity in social encounters.

We utilized three-dimensional radiative hydrodynamic simulations to model the evolution of massive young stellar objects, incorporating a variable reservoir of accreting material and several episodes of accretion inside a rotating, colliding-disc system. Factors that influence accretion patterns include: a movable upper boundary to simulate a range of disk sizes, variable disk colliding configurations, and a range of rotation rates. Enhancements in accretion rate lead to the formation of dense, rapidly converging streams that give rise to dense accretion hot spots at the center of the system, accelerating the merger of objects and influencing the final outcome of the system. In a system with a rapidly spinning core, enhancements in accretion rate can lead to the integration of a significant amount of material into the core, potentially leading to an explosive merger. The likelihood of these dense accretion phases depends on the stability of the system over time, with a majority of massive young stellar objects exhibiting multiple episodes of accretion. This suggests that massive stars often experience multiple episodes of accretion before reaching a state of balance, influencing their overall growth and evolution.

We investigate how water waves evolve over time, focusing on waves with long wavelengths and strong currents, particularly those that travel in both directions, known as counter-propagating waves. These waves can occur when there is a sudden impact, such as from an earthquake. Our research looks at how these waves change over time, especially how their shape distorts as they travel and interact with the water's surface. Specifically, we examined how these waves behave in response to an obstacle in the water's path, like a wall of rocks that juts out of the sea. Our findings are displayed through mathematical equations and illustrated with videos showing the movement of these waves over time.

The paper investigates the Stokes formula in a class of locally convex spaces that are equipped with a non-degenerate metric. To achieve this, the authors develop a version of the Stokes formula in a abstract setting, applying it to a broad range of operators, including differential forms, differential complexes, and de Rham cohomology. Specifically, the research demonstrates how the Stokes formula can be utilized to derive important properties of differential forms and to establish the existence and representation of differential forms in a broad range of spaces, including a class of locally convex spaces that are well-suited for analyzing analytical problems.

Autonomous navigation in unfamiliar environments can be complicated for robots due to the interplay between different navigation methods and sensor information.  This paper focuses on integrating a sonar sensor with a navigation system designed for floor transition scenarios.  After reviewing existing literature on navigation systems and sonar signal processing, the authors outline their integrated approach.  This approach utilizes a two-layered navigation controller with a upper layer featuring a floor expert controller and a lower layer with a path finding algorithm.  The controller's effectiveness is demonstrated through a test in which a robot transitions from a wooden to a concrete floor.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance compared to the current state of the art techniques.

This research investigates complex stimuli that incorporate linear trends, suggesting that the human visual system is highly sensitive to the curvature of these stimuli. To understand the specific challenge they pose, we analyzed them within a Gaussian linear filter model, varying the scale of the stimuli's standard deviation. Our findings indicate that the visual system easily processes curved patterns that resemble natural images but struggles with sharp curves, particularly in the periphery of the visual field. This difficulty is particularly pronounced for certain spatial frequencies found in natural images, which the human visual system exhibits a strong preference for filtering out. When we removed this preferred low-frequency information from complex stimuli, it significantly improved the performance of achromatic motion detection in the periphery. These results remain observable even when the complex stimuli are presented in high spatial resolution, suggesting that the bending effect has a significant bearing on the perception of natural images at the peripheral visual field.

We develop a new algorithm for projecting high-dimensional data onto a lower-dimensional space while removing the effects of rotational multiplicity and minimizing the impact of outliers. This results in a non-convex optimization problem with constant convergence rate guarantees, achieved through the application of advanced theoretical insights. Our approach involves an iterative process that combines block coordinate descent and the alternating projection algorithm, allowing for the efficient treatment of constraints and rotating coordinates. Our empirical studies demonstrate the premier performance of this method in real-world datasets.

Traditional information extraction from emotionally charged text, which necessitates identifying the intensity of positive or negative emotions, relies heavily on manual annotation. This process is notoriously labor-intensive, expensive, and subjective. To break down these barriers, we are introducing a new approach that leverages pre-trained BERT models to automate the review and correction of emotionally charged text annotations. At the heart of our method lies a robust, BERT-based emotion intensity estimation framework that compares the anxiety associated with given text and annotated labels. We collect and utilize a vast dataset of emotionally charged text and corresponding annotations to fine-tune the parameters of this framework. As a result, we are able to utilize this model to pinpoint erroneous annotations and propose corrected versions. To validate our approach, we conducted comparative experiments involving the incorporation of our method into a standard machine learning pipeline for emotionally charged text classification. The findings of these experiments reveal that our approach is capable of enhancing the accuracy of emotionally charged text classification systems that rely on manually created training datasets, in addition to demonstrating the utility of our annotation correction method for addressing the subjectivity inherent in emotionally charged text annotation.

For robots to effectively navigate complex, unfamiliar spaces safely and efficiently, they need a highly adaptable mapping strategy that balances exploration and optimization. In this paper, a novel approach is introduced that utilizes a unique, hierarchical representation of the environment's topology to guide decision-making. This novel method, called HiTMap, utilizes a holistic overview of the environment's layout and prioritizes the discovery of critical connectivity points, thereby optimizing path planning and exploration strategies. Compared to existing mapping and navigation approaches, HiTMap's performance is demonstrated to significantly outperform current methods in scenarios where the robot has a limited amount of time to explore the environment.

One of the key challenges in creating precise matter interferometry lies in finding reference frames that remain unaffected by external influences. As the interference pattern generated by matter depends on the relative phase, any variation in the reference frame will lead to a phase error and thus a measurement error. Typically, this issue is resolved by measuring the reference frame's fluctuations simultaneously with the interferometer's signal. Nevertheless, if the fluctuations could be made visible through an impact on the interferometer itself, it would essentially eliminate the need for a simultaneous measurement. Here, we present an unconventional use of atomic interferometry that achieves this exact result. By placing the interferometer within close proximity of a superconductor, the development of a magnetic field sensing capability is enabled through the Meissner effect, where the superconductor's response to the magnetic field will cause fluctuations in the atomic trajectory and thus a change in the interference pattern. This approach allows for the measurement of very small magnetic fields - specifically in the nanotesla range - and demonstrates the potential for atomic interferometry to be sensitive to local field conditions around the measurement site.

This study explores a type of finite mixture models where the underlying components belong to a parametric family dependent on a set of parameters, and assigns each observation to exactly one component based on the parameters. A key aspect of these models is that they incorporate uncertainty in the form of distributional estimates of the component parameters. A new method of estimating the number of components and their associated weights involves using non-parametric density estimates and results in an equivalent model with convex structure. A simulation demonstrates that this method yields nearly identical results to traditional approaches when the number of components is known. A important aspect of finite mixture models reveals itself in the context of overfitting, where models with multiple components can lead to increased model complexity. A notable example of such models involving multiple components includes hidden Markov models.

Due to the intricate physics engine simulation example, the case study for the DynaSOAr memory allocator includes 12 lines of code. The underlying programming model is in the C++ language, and the memory allocator is a part of the CUDA framework. In the context of GPU programming, memory allocation is typically managed automatically, thus overshadowing the underlying physics of memory on GPUs. However, by developing an own memory allocator for CUDA, we were able to gain a deeper understanding of memory on GPUs. The resulting DynaSOAr memory allocator exhibits superior performance, particularly when utilizing smaller data sets. The evidence from this experiment, in addition to previous research, shows that memory allocation can significantly impact performance in various GPU applications. Therefore, developers are encouraged to evaluate their system's specific circumstances and choose between manual and automatic memory management based on their particular needs. The efficient DynaSOAr memory allocator is now publicly available for other developers to utilize.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the detailed analysis of spin-resolved density of states and recognizes the crucial role of boundary effects within narrow superconducting materials. It also considers the critical alignment of the crystallographic orientation with the superconducting properties. Utilizing this model, the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states associated with a single manganese adatom were simulated, along with clusters of different sizes, positioned on the Nb(110) surface. The results revealed unique Yu--Shiba--Rusinov state patterns that are highly sensitive to the spatial arrangement of the manganese clusters and their individual sizes. Furthermore, the theory successfully correlated the experimental findings with the underlying electronic properties of the superconducting material and the spatial arrangement of the magnetic clusters.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young exoplanetary system, TOI-712, hosting four mini-Neptune sized planets around an $8.10\pm0.45$ day period star. By analyzing $TESS$ data, we determined the dimensions of the star to be $r_\star = 8.10\pm0.45$ $r_\sun$ and the surface temperature to be $T_\sun \pm 200 K$. Subsequent observations with the High-Resolution Spectrograph (HRS) on the $TESS$ satellite and a combination of spectroscopic and photometric techniques were used to derive the planetary sizes and densities. All four planets in the system have similar densities, suggesting they have the same composition. Three of the planets were found to have orbital periods of $8.10\pm0.45$ days, $11.97\pm0.01$ days, $24.52\pm0.02$ days, and an undetermined period for the fourth planet. By analyzing the stellar properties and the properties of the planets, we found that the surface gravity of the star is $log(g_\star) = 4.68\pm0.01$. Further research is needed to determine the eccentricity of the planets and to understand the effects of tidal interaction on the systems' evolution.

We examined the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen impurities in rutile TiO2 up to a distance of 6 rutile TiO2 layers from the dopant using density functional theory. Up to 4 layers, up to 3 layers showed significant bond length modification with bond angles affected deeper.  Up to 2 layers showed up down spin coupling depending on dopant type, with deeper layers exhibiting magnetic moment formation.  The magnitude of magnetic moment decreased with distance from the dopant but never reached zero.  Van der Waals surfaces showed that deeper layers had more complex structures with more pronounced peaks indicating more electron involvement.  Calculated formation energies showed that magnetism was more stable with N than C.  We address some discrepancies in previous research that found no magnetic properties in certain layers.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the effectiveness of this analysis for identifying the combination of top-quarks and a gluon at the Large Hadron Collider but note its inapplicability for detecting the combination of top-quarks and a photon. I also outline the potential for this analysis in the High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider and provide an initial estimate of achievable sensitivities.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin introduced the concept of upper richness within Ramsey theory, specifically focusing on upper bounded graphs. They established a concrete lower bound for this phenomenon, which we will refer to as the Erdos-Galvin bound. Subsequently, a set of researchers specified conditions under which the Erdos-Galvin bound is achievable within graphs comprising edges of infinite magnitude. In the course of our investigation, we identified an alternative, more accessible proof for this particular scenario. Moreover, we provide an innovative upper limit to the richness of graphs featuring edge weights from the set $\{1,2,\dots,k\}$, particularly for weights beyond the quantity $2k$-1. This, in turn, enables us to establish a lower bound for upper richness within graphs defined by the set of edges $\{1,2,\dots,k\}$, designated as $r_{RF}(k)$, which we find to be $2k-1$ for weights beyond $k=2$. Notably, this is comparable to the upper bound for diagonal Ramsey numbers over the set of edge weights $\{1,2,\dots,k\}$, which is $k^2$ for weights beyond $k=2$.

Our analysis highlights that certain types of noise, particularly qudit amplitude decay and dephasing, actually become beneficial in implementing a quantum circuit simulation of scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$D, specifically for calculating vacuum polarization. Quantifying the optimal noise intensity, we find it's essential for the noise to be non-Gaussian in order to efficiently simulate this model. Moreover, noise that scales with the operator norm can lead to a polynomial reduction in the required circuit depth, whereas noise bounded by the operator's trace norm leads to a linear reduction in required depth. Non-Gaussian noise also offers advantages over Gaussian noise when simulating other phenomena, such as electron-positron pair creation.

Researchers have demonstrated the generation of a highly concentrated beam of polarized positrons utilizing a thin layer of carbon film, which has been subjected to a strong laser beam interacting with a background of moderate strength. This achievement occurs within the context of quantum electrodynamics, a realm where the interaction between the positrons and intense light plays a significant role. It has been discovered that targets with higher density that are compact, yet not extremely small, produce the most intense positron beams, and that the degree of polarization reaches nearly 100% and remains nearly constant, even as the intensity of the electron-positron pair production increases significantly. This phenomenon is attributed to the pre-existing alignment of the atomic bonds within the crystalline targets, which remain unchanged as the positrons are generated. This discovery suggests that certain specific materials, particularly those with tightly bound atoms, may serve as efficient sources of polarized positrons, even for a wide range of intense light sources.

Given a finite group G and a subgroup H of G, we examine the structure of H when its left coset system is spanned by a polynomial of minimal degree relative to a given basis. Initially, we establish that if the smallest degree required is odd, then H must be a subgroup of G's normalizer relative to that basis. Furthermore, when the smallest degree is even, we demonstrate that the character theory of G incorporates an even number of non-zero irreducible characters relative to the given basis, allowing us to conclude that H is both a maximal subgroup and a normalizer of G relative to that basis.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature detector with a small footprint. The design employs a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to mitigate bias errors and provides two output voltages that change with temperature. A precise conversion formula is derived to calculate the temperature from the output values. The temperature detector was implemented in a 180nm process and characterized for temperatures between 25°C and 90°C. The design achieves high accuracy with a maximum inaccuracy of 1.4°C and offers a low power consumption of 120nW. The compact design has a small area of 20x20μm² and provides a high resolution of 0.24°C. The proposed design can be utilized in applications such as memory and storage devices.

We introduce a concept of geometric frameworks based on Lie groupoids and details how they correlate with Lie groupoids through a process called unfolding. Upshot: unfolding a geometric framework yields a Lie groupoid, and vice versa, with an inverse relationship known as folding. This inverse relationship is made precise by establishing it is a functor that reverses the process of unfolding. Additionally, we explore how unfolding and folding interact with morphisms between Lie groupoids and detail the applicability of this relationship to distinguishing isomorphic Lie groupoids.

We've analyzed a particular infrared dark cloud called G19.32+0.14, which is undergoing significant dynamical change as it's being affected by a nearby expanding HII region driven by a massive O-type star. Contrary to previous findings, our observations with the SMA and GBT reveal that the cloud's central dense core is actively engaging in accretion, likely as a result of external gravitational forces triggered by the star's influence. This is reflected in the core's increasing mass and rotational motion. Our data also indicate that the core's density has decreased, and it's slowly disintegrating as it moves away from the star. This research suggests that external factors, such as interactions with nearby HII regions and protostars, can influence the core's mass and shape, and may be a critical factor in the formation of low- and intermediate-mass stars.

We develop a one-step prediction method for linear random field models with spatially correlated errors, where the number of observations is equal to the number of parameters being estimated. Our approach involves inverting a Toeplitz matrix, which facilitates the use of fast Fourier transform techniques to efficiently compute predictions. We also examine the asymptotic behavior of our estimation procedure and contrast it with existing literature. Furthermore, we provide an illustrative example using R to demonstrate our method's practical application.

The interaction between textures, specifically the irregular surfaces of sponges or the human skin, and liquid foams exhibits significant diversity and is influenced by multiple factors including the type of soap, pressure, and surface geometry. To better understand this relationship, researchers created a sponge texture with uniform features and studied its interaction with soap bubbles using high-speed cameras and advanced pressure measurement technology. By analyzing these results alongside theoretical models, a deeper insight into the complex connection between the soap and sponge was gained, revealing that the friction between them varies significantly, even with small changes in the soap's surface energy. Furthermore, unusual phenomena observed during the experiment, such as the formation of bubbles within the sponge pores, were also understood through high-resolution imaging.

This study involves developing an efficient technique for identifying abnormal images in skin cancer datasets. Deep learning models can generate valuable features from images, and their use has become the standard in many applications. However, the presence of outlier images may negatively impact performance and necessitate their removal or correction. We extracted 15,000 skin cancer images from Google, removing 1,500 outliers determined to affect the results significantly. A combination of two techniques is proposed to detect and remove outliers: using a pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and calculating the entropy of output probabilities. We connect 7,000 training images to 8,000 detection ones and use the remaining 10,000 for validation and testing. The proposed method's effectiveness in detecting outliers is demonstrated by comparing the entropy of normal and abnormal images. The proposed approach, using only 2,000 training images, achieves an accuracy of 95.3% on the detection task and 91.5% when using 8,000 training images. The code for this project has been made available online.

The interaction between a rotating fluid and a less dense, chemically distinct gas that undergoes a spontaneous combustion reaction is being studied in a horizontal Hele-Shaw cell. When the inner surface of the cell is stimulated, the resulting pattern of the combustion reaction displays significant flexibility and can take on various forms, depending on the speed at which the inner surface of the cell is stimulated and the speed at which the cell is rotated. The observation of the combustion reaction pattern in this situation differs significantly from the pattern observed when the cell is not rotated. When the cell is not rotated, the combustion reaction pattern takes on a rectangular shape, regardless of the speed at which the inner surface of the cell is stimulated. The ability to stimulate the combustion reaction pattern in this situation in multiple ways also makes this situation different from a previous experiment where the inner surface of the cell was stimulated in a wavelike motion. The movement of the inner surface of the cell in that previous experiment caused the combustion reaction pattern to break into waves. The movement of the inner surface of the cell in the current experiment could be stopped before the combustion reaction pattern breaks into waves, which is not similar to the previous experiment. The pattern of the combustion reaction in this situation can be stopped and started again, which is unlike the previous experiment where the pattern of the combustion reaction could not be stopped and started again.
